Two of these leading actors included fellow car guys and racing drivers James Garner and Paul Newman.

Things got heated enough between McQueen and Garner that the latter wasn't shy about calling the former out after working together on the set of "The Great Escape." Newman wasn't so keen on McQueen, either. We'll explore these disagreements below, which still prompt movie and motorsport fans to compare the racing careers and accolades of all three Hollywood leading men, from Sebring to Le Mans.

Big actors have to spend their time (and money) off-screen doing something, right? In the case of Steve McQueen, Paul Newman, and James Garner, cars and motorsport were irresistible. McQueen managed to place second alongside Peter Revson at the 12 Hours of Sebring, coming in just behind the last American international racing legend himself, Mario Andretti. Newman's racing career spanned 35 years and a dozen championships as a driver and team owner. Garner was an Off-Road Motorsports Hall of Fame inductee who raced in everything from the Indianapolis 500 to the NORRA Mexican 1000.

You might think that would be enough to squash any set beef and keep things civil among petrolheads. Not so much. While Newman and McQueen were co-stars in the 1974 movie, "The Towering Inferno," the two reportedly hit a boiling point. Newman called the Bullitt star a "chickens**t" following McQueen's rage over Newman having 12 more lines than him. The two then feuded over billing on the film's posters and credits until the studio settled on double top billing.

Garner, even with his good guy repute in show business, had some choice words for McQueen, labeling the actor a "poser who cultivated the image of a macho man" after working with him on the set of "The Great Escape." Ouch. McQueen's behavior on "The Great Escape" also prompted Garner to say, "Steve could be a stubborn little cuss, but the director added some motorcycle stunts to pacify him and changed his character to a guy who goes out to reconnoiter the countryside then unselfishly allows himself to be recaptured so he can share information with others."

A love for all things fast, fun, and dangerous wasn't enough to keep McQueen from a strained relationship with Newman and Garner. If anything, the connection invited competition and frequent comparison. When it came to "The Towering Inferno" co-stars, famed racing driver Dick Barbour applauded both actors, but seemed to give the edge to McQueen for his talent. "Paul was a very methodical driver. He wasn't a natural like Steve. McQueen picked it up immediately," Barbour said . That's coming from a driver who spent time co-driving with Newman and coaching McQueen.

Granted, Garner and McQueen weren't co-stars on the track, but that didn't stop the former from impressing racing royalty. Bob Bondurant, the former Formula 1 racing driver and racing school founder, applauded Garner's skills in the 2006 documentary "Pushing the Limit: The Making of Grand Prix."

title: Trump’s DOE Budget Request Cuts Weak Bets And Useful Energy Research Together
raw_summary: There are Department of Energy programs in the Trump administration’s FY2027 budget request that I would cut too. Hydrogen for buses, trucks, building heat and routine electricity storage has consumed years of public funding and attention without overcoming the basic efficiency and cost advantages of using electricity directly. Ending more attempts to force those applications into existence would be progress. The problem is that the administration has wrapped those defensible cuts into a much broader retreat from batteries, electric vehicles, buildings, solar, wind and public energy research while treating several much weaker technological bets far more gently. Across thirteen selected DOE technology program lines, FY2026 enacted funding totals about $4.288 billion. Trump’s FY2027 request reduces that to $2.618 billion, a decline of roughly 39%. The distribution matters much more than the aggregate. Solar, wind, vehicles and buildings together fall from $1.005 billion to only $40 million, about a 96% reduction. These are selected annual DOE programs, not the entire department or every federal dollar that supports the technologies, and the FY2027 figures are a presidential request rather than enacted appropriations. But budget requests tell Congress what an administration thinks deserves public support, and the pattern is difficult to mistake.

article_paragraphs: There are Department of Energy programs in the Trump administration’s FY2027 budget request that I would cut too. Hydrogen for buses, trucks, building heat and routine electricity storage has consumed years of public funding and attention without overcoming the basic efficiency and cost advantages of using electricity directly. Ending more attempts to force those applications into existence would be progress. The problem is that the administration has wrapped those defensible cuts into a much broader retreat from batteries, electric vehicles, buildings, solar, wind and public energy research while treating several much weaker technological bets far more gently.

Across thirteen selected DOE technology program lines, FY2026 enacted funding totals about $4.288 billion. Trump’s FY2027 request reduces that to $2.618 billion, a decline of roughly 39%. The distribution matters much more than the aggregate. Solar, wind, vehicles and buildings together fall from $1.005 billion to only $40 million, about a 96% reduction. These are selected annual DOE programs, not the entire department or every federal dollar that supports the technologies, and the FY2027 figures are a presidential request rather than enacted appropriations. But budget requests tell Congress what an administration thinks deserves public support, and the pattern is difficult to mistake.

The useful way to judge these programs is not to divide technologies into politically favored and politically disfavored camps. Research, demonstrations and deployment support should face different tests. Early-stage research should answer a credible question that is worth answering. A demonstration should resolve specific technical, operating or commercial uncertainties. Deployment funding should accelerate something with a plausible path to delivering useful services competitively. A technology can justify a bounded experiment while being a terrible candidate for a billion-dollar rollout, and commercial success in a sector does not mean there are no remaining public-interest research questions.

Solar and wind illustrate the latter point. Their DOE program lines go from $220 million and $100 million respectively to zero in the FY2027 request. Neither technology requires the federal government to prove that it can generate electricity at commercial scale. That argument was settled years ago. The remaining public questions concern durability, manufacturing, recycling, materials, grid integration and operating electricity systems with very large shares of variable generation. Firms should fund ordinary product competition, but shared knowledge and system-level research often produce benefits that no single company can capture.

Vehicles fall from $397 million to $20 million, while buildings fall from $288 million to $20 million. That is especially difficult to square with the actual transition. Battery-electric vehicles have already won substantial passenger-vehicle markets and are spreading rapidly into commercial-duty niches where economics align. Heat pumps are a mature technology whose remaining problems increasingly concern installation quality, controls, building integration, flexible demand and how to electrify existing buildings without making unnecessary renovation a prerequisite. Those are exactly the kinds of practical problems that public research can help solve across an industry.

Hydrogen is a different case. The annual hydrogen and fuel-cell line falls from $160 million to zero, and much of its energy mission deserves to disappear. Producing hydrogen, conditioning it, moving it and converting it back into useful work generally adds energy losses, equipment and cost compared with direct electrification. Necessary industrial hydrogen is different because ammonia, methanol and other chemical processes require the molecule itself. A sensible federal portfolio would focus its hydrogen expertise on reducing emissions from hydrogen that industry actually needs while ending serial attempts to create a giant new hydrogen market for applications where electricity already has the advantage.

That does not mean the much larger regional hydrogen hubs have simply been cancelled. The hubs are multiyear awards funded separately from the annual technology-program comparison, and five remained nominally retained after the administration’s review. Retention, however, is not the same thing as a functioning project. Reporting from Pennsylvania continues to describe uncertainty, cautious partners and little evidence of meaningful momentum, while the FY2027 request proposes clawing back unobligated clean-hydrogen funding. The result is less a coherent technology decision than a prolonged “will they or won’t they?” process that makes planning harder for good projects and bad projects alike.

The mixed treatment of other technologies reinforces the point. Critical-minerals funding rises sharply, from $83 million to $364 million, and some of that can be useful if it builds processing, refining and qualified industrial output rather than merely subsidizing extraction. Geothermal remains at $150 million, including substantial support for enhanced-geothermal work whose eventual electricity economics remain uncertain. Civilian nuclear falls only about 9%, from $1.685 billion to $1.534 billion. Existing-fleet work and bounded research can have value without accepting the proposition that new nuclear or SMRs are likely to become the fast, inexpensive backbone of the transition.

title: Who Killed The Elon Musk Movie? Nope, Not That Billionaire, Must Be Another One

article_paragraphs: Tesla CEO and well known billionaire Elon Musk has made quite a journey since 2004, when he joined Martin Eberhardt and Marc Tarpenning as the lead investor in their EV startup Tesla Motors. All of it, and more, is captured in the new documentary film, “Musk,” It was set to open on 472 screens across the country on Friday, October 16, but if you blinked, you missed it. The film’s distributor, Bleecker Street, has already pulled it out of action. Well, timing is everything…

Leading up to last week’s blackout, the “Musk” documentary was riding high on a cushion of supportive publicity, with acclaimed documentary filmmaker Alex Gibney at the helm and Elon Musk providing a fascinating, high profile subject in the great tradition of the US auto industry.

Among other works, Gibney was a consulting producer on the hard-hitting 2006 documentary directed by Chris Paine, “Who Killed the Electric Car?” The film excoriated General Motors for killing off its 199o’s-era EV1 electric sedan after just a few years at low-volume production. The car was leased, not sold, and only a few escaped the junkyard crusher when GM halted production and recalled the vehicles.

With that in his background, Gibney might be expected to create a somewhat flattering portrait of the little known young investor who made the Tesla Motors dream come true. In fact, Paine eneded “Who Killed the Electric Car” with a shot of a Tesla prototype. Paine also went on to direct the 2011 sequel “Revenge of the Electric Car” featuring Tesla along with GM and other EV-curious automakers.

Musk himself gave the sequel a glowing review on social media back in 2019. “ Great electric car documentary about early days of Tesla, GM Volt, Nissan Leaf & Gadget. So much has happened since then,” Musk inscribed on Twitter, the social media site he acquired in 2022.

Yes, so much has happened since then. Gibney is well known for his deep dives into American entrepreneurs run amok and other topics dealing with dark side of success and power in the hands of ethically bankrupt people, almost all of them men (Gibney’s 2019 HBO documentary on the now-imprisoned Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes is one notable exception).

In “Musk,” Gibney takes another crack at the power nexus so deftly wielded by Elon Musk, all the way on up to the entrepreneur’s post as chief chainsaw-wielder at US President Donald Trump’s “DOGE” budget-cutting office.

“Musk” also fills the gaps in Musk’s home life, including interviews with the mothers of his 14 or so children, which presumably makes for juicy viewing. That helps explain why Bleecker Street was aiming for a wide release, a rather unusual plan for a long-format documentary totaling almost four hours. So unusual, in fact, that Bleecker Street pulled the plug after just one week.

article_paragraphs: If you have ever shopped for catalytic converters or aftermarket performance parts, you might have noticed that some parts are listed as "C.A.R.B. compliant" and others as "49-state" or "Federally legal." And you probably noticed that the C.A.R.B. legal parts are way more expensive than their federally legal equivalents. This is because C.A.R.B., or the California Air Research Board, sets stricter emissions standards for vehicles than the rest of the country. As such, any aftermarket parts that affect the emissions system need to be C.A.R.B. certified. This means manufacturers need to prove that their parts do not increase a vehicle's emissions or face hefty fines like Cobb Tuning did a few years ago.

Parts makers may be tempted to tell the Golden State to kick rocks and not sell parts there, but California registers 1.8 million cars and trucks annually. To ignore that market would be to ignore one of the biggest new car markets in the U.S. So, in order to sell parts to Californians, manufacturers must go through an intensive testing process to make their parts C.A.R.B. legal.

An aftermarket performance part installed anywhere from the intake to the catalytic converter can affect emissions equipment in the eyes of the EPA. This applies to air intakes, ECU tunes, headers, non-OEM replacement catalytic converters, and superchargers. For an emissions-related part to be legal in California, it needs an Executive Order (EO) from C.A.R.B. An EO is basically a paperwork trail that proves the part does not increase emissions and is exempted from emissions anti-tampering laws.

A manufacturer must file the right paperwork with C.A.R.B. and have emissions testing performed at an approved lab in order to obtain an EO. If you think that the extra paperwork and testing sounds time consuming and expensive, you'd be right. But if the part passes, it is issued an EO number that is unique to a specific application (e.g., an air intake for a 2015 to 2017 Ford Mustang with the 5.0-liter V8). C.A.R.B. approved parts come with a sticker or tag displaying the EO number so emissions testers can verify that the part is compliant. If a part has an EO number but isn't installed in the right car, or if an EO part is modified, it is illegal, and your car won't pass emissions testing.

The benefit of C.A.R.B. approved parts is that you can increase your car's horsepower without increasing its emissions or running afoul of the law. However, the downside is often increased cost. For example, in California and other states following the C.A.R.B. standard, aftermarket catalytic converters must last 5 years or 50,000 miles. The EPA standard is 2 years or 24,000 miles. To meet this standard, the California-legal converters need more of the rare precious metals, like platinum, palladium, and rhodium, that convert an engine's toxic exhaust into something more benign.

It may seem strange that a state agency has such a considerable influence on the environmental regulations of the U.S. But the authority C.A.R.B. wields is not an accident and didn't happen overnight. Smog, the toxic byproduct of unburnt fuel from cars mixing with nitrogen oxides, was a huge problem in the U.S., particularly after the population and economic boom following World War II. California had some of the worst air quality in the nation, due to its growing population, reliance on cars, and climate and topography.

On especially bad days, the thick smog caused bad eye and lung irritation, and visibility was down to just a few blocks. Because the air was so bad, California was the first state to regulate vehicle emissions in 1966. But it wasn't until 1967 that C.A.R.B. was created to unify the state's approach to fighting smog. When the the EPA was established, federal regulators largely deferred to California when setting regulations because the state was already ahead of the game when it came to controlling car emissions. Also, due to then governor Ronald Regan's petitioning, California was able to retain its ability to set stricter emission standards than the rest of the country.

C.A.R.B. and its ability to set different standards than the rest of the country remain controversial, with the Trump administration repeatedly attempting to strike down California's emissions standards . But without some of the emissions technology that California has championed through regulation, like positive crankcase ventilation (PCV) systems, catalytic converters, and onboard diagnostics, our air would certainly be a lot dirtier.

article_paragraphs: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility !

U.S. federal safety regulators continue to tackle the sticky problem of autonomous vehicles, this time with a proposal that could signal to the public, quite literally, when a vehicle is operating autonomously.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has proposed new lighting requirements for autonomous vehicles that include an option (dare I say a strong suggestion?) to use cyan-colored lights to signal when a vehicle is operating autonomously without a human occupant monitoring the road.
The agency is not proposing a mandate for blue-green lights. Importantly, under the proposal, the lights would be used when an AV is operating in autonomous mode.
Still, federal regulators are clearly seeking some uniform way of identifying autonomous vehicles.

The proposal establishes equipment specifications, including where the lights are mounted, the color they emit, and how they’re activated. It would also remove requirements for manually operated controls for turn signals, high beams, and hazard lights.
Under the proposal, the NHTSA suggests the lights be cyan (blue-green), remain steadily illuminated rather than flash, and be visible from the front, rear, and both sides.
This latest proposal is one piece of a bigger effort to update regulations that help speed up the adoption of AVs while maintaining safety, according to NHTSA administrator Jonathan Morrison.

title: The Bugatti Veyron Super Sport Prototype's Power Increase Exploded The A/C Compressor
raw_summary: Once you're operating at the very edge of what's possible with a road car, there's no such thing as a minor tweak. On a normal car, a tire is just a tire. At 200-plus mph, it's a countdown timer. The Bugatti Veyron's Michelin tires, which used the same PAX run-flat tech as Honda's Odyssey minivan , were good for roughly 15 minutes at 250 mph, and then they were done. Nothing at that level is forgiving because every part is already working as hard as it can, and changing one thing drags a dozen others along with it. Just ask Bugatti. article_paragraphs: Once you're operating at the very edge of what's possible with a road car, there's no such thing as a minor tweak. On a normal car, a tire is just a tire. At 200-plus mph, it's a countdown timer. The Bugatti Veyron's Michelin tires, which used the same PAX run-flat tech as Honda's Odyssey minivan , were good for roughly 15 minutes at 250 mph, and then they were done.

Nothing at that level is forgiving because every part is already working as hard as it can, and changing one thing drags a dozen others along with it. Just ask Bugatti. The original Veyron made 1,001 horsepower and topped out at 253 mph. It was already the fastest production car on the planet, so there was no easy margin left to borrow.

Getting from there to the 1,200-hp Super Sport, which hit 267.8 mph, took Bugatti two and a half years of development for a 20 percent jump in output. The Super Sport was so extensively re-engineered compared with the original Veyron 16.4 that, in many respects, it was practically a new car. The tub lost 77 pounds, and Bugatti reworked most of the car's essential systems.

And the proof came early. In a standard Veyron, the 1,200-hp engine destroyed the A/C compressor. Yes, the air conditioning. Think of it as the canary in the coal mine, except the canary was the climate control. Nobody expects cabin cooling to be the weak link on a hypercar, but a part doesn't have to be glamorous to hit its limit. Here's a look at the changes it took to turn the Veyron into the Super Sport, and how that pushed an already extreme car even further.

The compressor's job is to raise the refrigerant's pressure; the condenser then dumps the heat, and the refrigerant goes on to chill the cabin. The Veyron's A/C system also gets its own radiator, the tenth on the car, plus two condensers fed by intakes in the nose. In most cars, a belt connects the crankshaft to a pulley on the compressor.

With the A/C running, a clutch locks the compressor to that pulley, so its speed rises and falls with the engine's. That's the connection to the Veyron's failure. On the Super Sport, peak power moved from 6,000 to 6,400 rpm and torque rose from 922 lb-ft to 1,106 lb-ft. Jason Cammisa, writing for Road & Track , blames an engine that "spun so quickly from idle to redline in first gear." In his earlier MotorTrend feature, he wrote that the A/C system "couldn't bleed off pressure quickly enough."

Things like this can happen when you're engineering a 1,200-horsepower car, something very few engineers likely had ever attempted before the Super Sport. And the challenges went well beyond the engine. Even the tires had to be specially engineered to withstand the speeds Bugatti was chasing with the Veyron and Chiron .

The Chiron kept the Veyron's 8.0-liter, four-turbo W16 layout and took it to 1,500 horsepower. Its A/C compressor is rated for up to 10 kW of cooling, which Bugatti conveniently compares to chilling a European apartment of roughly 860 square feet, and the Pur Sport's engine revs to 6,900 rpm. It's tempting to read that as a lesson from the Super Sport, but we'll likely never know.

We put down about $4,000 and leased a Kia EV6 for an astounding $137 a month. Our household cell phone bill runs that rate. That two-year lease was even extended for another six months, for a completely manageable $148 per month. There were a few factors in our favor regarding that deal. First, there were, of course, the $7,500 Biden incentives. New York State added another $2,000 discount on top of that. Additionally, when we locked in this lease, carmakers had miscalculated market demand, with a glut that began in 2023. Dealers finance their inventories; the longer they sit unsold, the deeper they go into the red. So even though our EV6 Light Long Range Wind stickered for $51,845, we got it (well, use of it) for dirt cheap.

article_paragraphs: Back in 2024, long before the Trump White House murdered the $7,500 tax credit for EVs , my wife and I locked in an insanely good deal on a lease. We put down about $4,000 and leased a Kia EV6 for an astounding $137 a month. Our household cell phone bill runs that rate. That two-year lease was even extended for another six months, for a completely manageable $148 per month.

There were a few factors in our favor regarding that deal. First, there were, of course, the $7,500 Biden incentives. New York State added another $2,000 discount on top of that. Additionally, when we locked in this lease, carmakers had miscalculated market demand, with a glut that began in 2023. By September of 2024, dealers struggled to sell EVs fast enough, stuck with electric cars for an average of over three months compared to a somewhat healthier 79 days for gas cars. Dealers finance their inventories; the longer they sit unsold, the deeper they go into the red. So even though our EV6 Light Long Range Wind stickered for $51,845, we got it (well, use of it) for dirt cheap.

That was then. As of this fall, with our lease expiring, I was eyeing new EVs, but not liking prices. Cox Automotive says the average sticker on a new electric whip in September hit an eye-watering $55,879. Still, have you seen gas prices? We wanted to stay electric. Fortunately, used EV prices are much lower. At the time of my research, I saw CarGurus ' price tracking showed the 2023 Chevy Bolt selling at an average tab of $20,518; the 2024 EV6 at $27,846; and the 2023 Hyundai Ioniq 5 at $27,436.

My goal was to find the right used Ioniq 5. That was the car I wanted back in 2024, but there were better deals on the EV6. No shade to the Kia; we've loved it. But we dug the Ioniq 5's retro-futuristic styling more, and it's a little bit shorter, so it fits better in our very cramped garage.

The rub? We didn't want to spend more than we would've on a used Honda Civic, which CarGurus showed running at $23,967 for a 2023 at the time of my analysis. With the 2023 Ioniq 5 averaging $27,436, that's a $3,469 average premium over the Honda. The 2023 Bolt is already cheaper than the Civic, but we liked the bigger Ioniq 5 and its all-wheel-drive availability.

Maybe you're less price-sensitive. But on most folks' budgets, if you're buying a used or new EV, you really have to get close to price parity with the gas car for the costs to pencil out. I recently wrote that energy costs still matter more than falling EV prices . The point of that story is that even though gas prices have shown increases exceeding 30% in a year while home electricity rates have only risen by about 5%, if you're paying thousands more on an EV, it's going to take years to recoup the higher outlay.

I didn't want to go into the hole on financing a more expensive car only to get pennies back per mile on the relatively cheaper cost of fueling an EV. Here's just a little bit of the math of this, because it's important to understand the cost burden of a more expensive electric car, even if it's cheaper to fuel.

The easiest way to see the apples-to-apples comparison of fueling costs, and, in turn, the payback time for spending more on an EV, is to measure that tab over 100 miles. On the gas car, that's 100 divided by the MPG of the car in question, multiplied by the price of a gallon of gas. This calculation gives you how many gallons you'll burn and the cost to purchase them. For EVs, you need the kilowatt-hour-per-100-mile rating of the EV you're shopping for, which you can find on fueleconomy.gov . Multiply that number by the kWh price where you live, which gives you something like the fueling-equivalent cost to drive that EV 100 miles versus the gas-car price.

title: Inside COTA's Turn 1 clubhouse and its plans to build a second track
raw_summary: For spectators and TV viewers tuning into coverage of F1's US Grand Prix, it's been hard to miss. Turn 1 of the Circuit of the Americas has a distinctly different look to it this year with the addition of a mammoth multi-storey clubhouse. Connected to the main paddock area via a cable car that crosses the track, this weekend the new hospitality structure serves as an extension of F1's swanky Paddock Club. From January 2 it becomes a year-round members-only club, dubbed 'The Circuit', as the venue turns private at the start of next year. "It isn’t an annual membership in the traditional sense," says Parris Mullins, COTA’s Senior Vice President of Motorsports. It’s much more like a country club. There are annual dues to maintain the facilities and cover staffing, but the initiation fee is a one-time payment that essentially provides a lifetime membership.

"It isn’t an annual membership in the traditional sense," says Parris Mullins, COTA’s Senior Vice President of Motorsports. It’s much more like a country club. There are annual dues to maintain the facilities and cover staffing, but the initiation fee is a one-time payment that essentially provides a lifetime membership.

"We’ve had more than 50 additional submissions in the past 24 hours, and that was before this race weekend. Before this race weekend, around 600 people had reached out. We’ve had one-to-one conversations with approximately 140 of them, and many have started putting down deposits and signing contracts.
"There will never be more than 300 members. We’re limiting North American membership to 250. The remaining 50 places will be a mix of international and corporate memberships."

The new facility isn't just COTA president Bobby Epstein's brainchild alone, though. It fits a calendar-wide push by F1 management for races to significantly ramp up their hospitality offerings. "A lot of our contract renewal was dependent on this as well," Mullins adds. "We needed to improve both the members’ experience and the experience for the Paddock Club guests. F1 has made a big commitment to it. The sport has grown, and certain markets demand these kinds of amenities. They have to keep improving what they offer."

COTA's decision to go private has some side effects, with the venue now no longer available for track days or for regional driving clubs. But there's a solution on the horizon. On an empty plot of land to the north of the existing F1 track, COTA has crafted advanced plans to build a second, shorter circuit designed for both cars and motorcycles.

"A second track will be built, primarily because we recognise that we’re displacing a number of people and organisations that have been partners of ours since the circuit opened," Mullins explains. "Growing motorsport, particularly in the local area, is very important to us. We’re not going to build another FIA Grade 1 facility because there’s no need for one. Instead, we want to build something that suits the local motorsport community, allows them to continue using a circuit and gives them access at a much lower price point.

"There’s obviously prestige associated with COTA. I know people love being able to say they’ve driven their car on the Grand Prix circuit, and we’re sorry that this won’t always be possible unless they’re members. But we want to give people somewhere they can drive, enjoy motorsport and continue participating at a grassroots level."

raw_title: How A Slick Ford Maverick Lobo Taught Me The True Meaning Of Truck Ownership
title: How A Slick Ford Maverick Lobo Taught Me The True Meaning Of Truck Ownership
raw_summary: I thought living in Detroit would be relatively safe in the coming climate crisis thanks to our fresh water and temperate climate. No real natural disasters routinely threaten this pleasant peninsula besides the slow-moving one of the freeze-thaw cycle every winter. Then, the night before I drove a 2027 Ford Maverick Lobo 300 miles on a mini-road trip to retrieve oil wrestling supplies in Ohio, my hometown was hit with its first tornado in 29 years. Suddenly, I was huddled with my three dogs in my basement, watching the lights flicker. I thought of Gary, Indiana. I thought of Flint. I thought of the U.S.'s de-funding of FEMA and rollback of regulations and rejection of anything that might save us, and then I thought, absolutely nothing is stopping me from using that Maverick Lobo to pick up 16 gallons of mineral oil and 300 pounds of bentonite now. Pickup ownership always seemed like a drag to me. They aren't particularly fun to drive, and if you're the average truck owner your bed remains empty most of the time until, inevitably, your days off start getting booked up by friends moving house. And I will admit to seeing one too many selfish truck drivers in my time. I started associating the entire vehicle type with self-centered behavior.

I thought of the U.S.'s de-funding of FEMA and rollback of regulations and rejection of anything that might save us, and then I thought, absolutely nothing is stopping me from using that Maverick Lobo to pick up 16 gallons of mineral oil and 300 pounds of bentonite now.

Pickup ownership always seemed like a drag to me. They aren't particularly fun to drive, and if you're the average truck owner your bed remains empty most of the time until, inevitably, your days off start getting booked up by friends moving house. And I will admit to seeing one too many selfish truck drivers in my time. I started associating the entire vehicle type with self-centered behavior.

That was until I heard the call for community building, with this little truck as the tool. Any car can be what you make of it. I learned that owning a truck can be an act of responsibility to the people around you, one that supplies joy rather than tiresome stress.
Full disclosure: Ford loaned me a Maverick Lobo with a full tank of gas to do with as I pleased for a week.

To be fair, the Ford Maverick Lobo does not scream "reliable citizen," especially when it's as low to the ground and blacked-out as this particular truck. And with a starting price of $41,425, and my tester topping out at $44,175, it's not exactly what I'd call a truck of the people. An unadorned base Maverick, however, squeaks in under $30,000, which these days is practically a steal.

The Lobo is Ford's "street truck" version of its money-printing little unibody ute, but it comes with the same turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4 EcoBoost engine as the base XT. Gas mileage was pretty good on my road trip (I scored about 28.1 mpg), but it's clear the "street" part of this street truck is more about the looks than packing in extra power. It's a little lower, the suspension is a little stiffer, the handling is a little sportier, and the 7-speed automatic shifts a little quicker over the base Maverick. It remains as easy to drive as a crossover, artfully maneuvering into city parking spots and in and out of traffic, but handles a little more like a sports car, all while having a useful bed on the back. Truly, it's a vehicle for all seasons. Mine also came with trailer assist, which, lol. I'm sure someone is hauling something with their Lobo, but I can't imagine it.

The day after the wild storm, my side of town was as it should be, but as I headed south and east, things became more fraught. The fragments of a city block lay across four roadways. Traffic lights blinked in abstract warning or stayed dark entirely. And then there was the rain. Constant torrents of rain, all the way from Detroit, to Cleveland, and back again.

Seven hours of solo driving in total, for folks I barely knew at the time. So, why did I do it? Well, I didn't need to know them. A friend of a friend reposted a call for anyone with the ability to pick up the oil for the event (and the mud for the following week), and I just happened to have the ability. Plus, I knew that the folks organizing the event were trying to create space in my community among people who needed it with nothing more than a pair of blow-up pools, a sign-in sheet and mineral oil. Despite the city's resurgence, Detroit folks still don't have a lot, and queer folks have even less. As a member of both communities, I happened to have access to a vehicle like a truck and could offer it to good people in need. If you can, do.

raw_title: Ford Patents Idea That Lets Parked Cars Autonomously Flee Danger
title: Ford Patents Idea That Lets Parked Cars Autonomously Flee Danger
raw_summary: It’s usually not a good sign when you park your car and then return to that spot to find it’s not where you left it. An idea in a recently published Ford patent application would turn that into a positive, though, as it would mean the vehicle sensed trouble and autonomously re-parked itself somewhere it deemed safer. The patent also describes ways to park and safeguard specific pieces of vehicle equipment—such as the wheels—and what you’re carrying inside or in a pickup’s bed. A Ford patent application submitted to the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) explains that a vehicle would detect “suspicious activity” and relocate itself somewhere less sketchy. Examples of these potential threats include a person who keeps peering into the windows or another vehicle repeatedly circling. The system could also decide a new spot is in order if the car finds itself alone in a previously populated lot—our four-wheeled friends get lonely too.

raw_title: 8 Classic Coupes That Look Sick With Window Louvers
title: 8 Classic Coupes That Look Sick With Window Louvers
raw_summary: Window louvers used to be a big deal on muscle cars for a reason that was actually two reasons: the cool factor. They made the car aesthetically cooler on the outside, and they also made it literally cooler on the inside, blocking some of the sun from coming in from those sweeping rear windows during a time when air conditioning was less universal. Those little side quarter louvers over the rear windows count, too, by the way. On top of the visual factor, they were good at decreasing the amount of sun hitting the rear passengers in exchange for increasing blind spots. But we're not here to try and convince anyone of the practical benefits of window louvers. Every car we're talking about today has been out of production for decades, and you're not here for the finer points of louver functionality. You're here for classic coupes that look awesome and are really hard to see out the back of. From muscle car royalty like the Plymouth 'Cuda through poster cars like the Datsun 280Z and multiple generations of Mustangs, we've got the goods. Here are eight cars that best wore those sick horizontal slats.

From muscle car royalty like the Plymouth 'Cuda through poster cars like the Datsun 280Z and multiple generations of Mustangs, we've got the goods. Here are eight cars that best wore those sick horizontal slats.

The first generation of the Ford Mustang Mach 1 arrived for the 1969 model year with its long, sloping roof and muscular proportions that looked fast when standing still. This was the first time that the Mach 1 moniker had shown up on a production car –- previously it was used on a fastback concept that Ford had been showing off at car shows, but now it had landed as a new Mustang variant with a wildly aggressive aesthetic. That first Mach 1 leaned hard into the visual excess, with enough graphics, stripes, exposed hood pins, and scoops to make an AutoZone cashier blush, and you'd better believe that included rear louvers.

Those louvers were called "Sport Slats," and they were a Ford factory option that promised to deliver a fast, sporty look to the back of the car and indeed did exactly that. Ford claimed at the time that the slats would keep sun glare and precipitation off of the rear glass, in fact improving rearward visibility, which feels like a stretch for something essentially styled off of half-closed venetian blinds. Regardless, they were a perfect finishing touch for a car that was already rocking more than its share of visual attitude and, while technically optional, they're an option you probably unconsciously select when you picture a first-gen Mach 1 in your head.

Far more than just an old-school pony car that isn't the Ford Mustang , the Plymouth Barracuda was one of the defining muscle cars of its era, specifically the now-iconic third-generation redesign that landed in 1970 and ran through 1974. The 'Cuda looked great, and there was plenty of performance underneath the styling, from the base 335-horsepower 383-cubic-inch V8 to the now-legendary 425-hp 426 big-block Hemi. It was a serious machine.

However, it also featured some arguably unserious styling choices, with Chrysler offering what they called "High Impact" paint colors like an alarming green and bold orange, along with graphics and additional options like a shaker hood. And yes, window louvers were on the menu, too. For example, the factory-installed Backlight Louver Package for 1971 matched a black vinyl roof with rear-window trim and racing mirrors, with a strange catch for unlucky buyers in exactly one state: The package was prohibited on cars registered in Pennsylvania. Pennsylvania's regulations explicitly prohibit "louvered materials" that obstruct visibility by more than 50% (told you so, Ford). However, we'd like to think they thought it should be illegal to look so cool.

If you wanted a pony car in 1970, Detroit's Big Three offered no shortage of options, but America's kookiest car company, AMC , was also in the mix, offering buyers a distinctive alternative despite being an automaker better known at the time for uninspired commuters. The AMC Javelin represented a serious effort to earn a place within the segment. AMC had poached racing legends Mark Donohue and Roger Penske away from Chevrolet, and Donohue determined that for the Javelin to compete on the high-speed Trans-Am racing series tracks, it would need a lot more downforce.

We point this out not because of a commitment to aerodynamic engineering in early-'70s racing, but because their solution –- a fat ducktail spoiler later available on the production car –- helped the Javelin look awesome. And while the spoiler landed in consumer showrooms for homologation reasons, there was nothing regulatory or even particularly useful about another exterior element that could help make the Javelin look as mean as its name: killer rear-window louvers. AMC never offered these as an option, but owners who decided to add them found that they give the already distinctive coupe an even more aggressive look through the back end, for an appearance that makes it look ready to pick a fight with anything wearing a Mustang badge.
bullet_points: Window louvers used to be a big deal on muscle cars for a reason that was actually two reasons: the cool factor.

They made the car aesthetically cooler on the outside, and they also made it literally cooler on the inside, blocking some of the sun from coming in from those sweeping rear windows during a time when air conditioning was less universal.

Holden showed the Monaro to the press for the first time at Surfers Paradise Raceway in Queensland on July the 22nd, 1968. 11 weeks later, a privately entered Monaro GTS 327 won the Hardie-Ferodo 500 at Bathurst. Essentially Australia’s equivalent to the Indy 500. It was Holden’s first ever win in the race, and it wouldn’t be the last.

The Monaro is one of the most iconic Australian cars ever made, it was an antipodean answer to wildly popular cars of the time, like the Mustang, Camaro, Javelin, Cougar, Firebird, Barracuda, and AMX. Image courtesy of General Motors Holden.

Ford’s XR Falcon GT, a four-door sedan with a 225 bhp version of the Mustang’s 289 cubic inch (4.7 liter) V8, had finished 1st and 2nd in the Hardie-Ferodo 500 race at Bathurst in 1967 – by far the biggest race in Australia.

At Ford’s archrival Holden, managing director Max Wilson and marketing director John Bagshaw pushed a two-door version of the new HK sedan range into production. Their case was easier to make because the coupe shared much of its body with the sedan, therefore development costs would be low and the development timeline would be short.

Bagshaw also argued for Chevrolet’s 327 V8 so the car could take on the Falcon GT both on the track and on dealership showroom floors. Holden needed a real halo car, and the Monaro would soon become the Australian automaker’s most iconic (and desirable) model.

The shape of the new coupe came from Holden’s newly-built design center at Fishermans Bend in Melbourne. Ted Schroeder blended the roof into the rear fenders in a way that echoed the 1966 Oldsmobile Toronado, though it left rear passengers with almost no view out. Holden called the result the first sports machine designed and engineered in Australia.

title: Here Are Five Cheaper Alternatives To Driving A Big Diesel Truck
raw_summary: The current state of fueling your diesel pickup in America is positively abysmal. With the national average holding steady at over six dollars for a gallon, and some places on the West Coast seeing pricing above eight dollars, it's never been more expensive to simply drive around. Even my relatively light, aerodynamic, and efficient Porsche Cayenne Diesel is suffering under the weight of $200 fill-ups at the moment. An absurd ongoing war with Iran is holding all of us hostage at the fuel pumps, and there's no amount of importing oil from Russia, selling "red diesel" for road use , or short-term fuel tax holidays that can ease the pain. There are plenty of reasons for buying a diesel truck or SUV, but these reasons tend to get less convincing as the cost of driving rises exponentially. I bought my Cayenne because I thought I would be towing a whole lot more than I actually am, but fuel costs (along with the inflationary response of the market) are pricing me out of the motorcycle track days I promised myself in the spring that I would be doing all summer. My recent trip to Alaska was budgeted for about half what I ended up spending on fuel, to the tune of hundreds of dollars.

I bought my Cayenne because I thought I would be towing a whole lot more than I actually am, but fuel costs (along with the inflationary response of the market) are pricing me out of the motorcycle track days I promised myself in the spring that I would be doing all summer. My recent trip to Alaska was budgeted for about half what I ended up spending on fuel, to the tune of hundreds of dollars.

I think the time has come to turn our backs on diesel and try to figure out an alternative. Maybe you still need your truck for heavy-duty hauling and towing jobs, which is what they're built for. But the truck should serve as a tool to be used sparingly, supplemented by something more fuel efficient when the Super Duty doesn't call. Here are some money-saving alternatives for your next trip that will help you get where you need to be without paying big bucks to get there.

I'm not saying you have to immediately give up your truck and buy something electric, but there has never been a better time to get a used EV. If you can fit one into your life, they can be excellent transportation tools . Used prices are up slightly for EVs in the last few months, but there's still a pretty good supply of them out there and, for the most part, they're much less expensive than they once were. The American charging infrastructure is robust and relatively easy to figure out. More than anything, EVs are incredibly cheap to drive and maintain.

Let's look at a real-world example. My 2013 Porsche Cayenne Diesel returns an observed average of about 29 mpg in the real world. With Ohio's current statewide average gallon price at $6.06, that translates to about 21 cents per mile of driving, not accounting for increasing maintenance, insurance, and registration costs. A modern electric commuter, say a new base model Nissan Leaf, achieves around 3 miles per kilowatt-hour of electricity. The average residential rate of electricity in Ohio is 18.04 cents per kWh, meaning that each of those miles costs about 6 cents. This is a bit of an apples to oranges comparison when it comes to each vehicle's capabilities, but purely for cost of driving, the Leaf is a clear advantage. Driving the Cayenne 10,000 miles costs $2,100 in fuel, while the same mileage in the Leaf is just $600.

If you aren't ready for a full EV experience, driving a plug-in hybrid can deliver similar fuel savings around town, and the gasoline engine allows you to continue driving long-distance as though it were a regular gas car. It's kind of the best of both worlds. In a two-vehicle household, it typically makes financial sense to have one with a plug.

You might remember hearing some scuttle about waste vegetable oil conversions for diesel vehicles back during the 2008 financial crisis. People were looking for ways to reduce their spending and found that the proliferation of fried fast food throughout the nation was potentially a good source of fuel. The used oil from a deep fryer could be filtered and burned in a diesel vehicle almost as though it were fresh out of the pump .

Sometimes restaurants will just give it to you, as they're required to pay someone to cart it away for recycling, but if enough people in your area start needing WVO for their diesels, the restaurants (or opportunistic employees) may start charging for the privilege. Even at a buck a gallon, you're getting it significantly cheaper than at the pump. You will also need to build yourself a purifying filter system at home, which can be messy and dangerous.

title: What The Numbers And "W" On Engine Oil Mean
raw_summary: Is your motor oil rated to handle all the conditions your car will experience? You don't need an engineering degree to drive a car, but sometimes it can feel like you need one to buy engine oil for it . Either that or proficiency in some language you don't yet understand. Because engine oil doesn't just come in one type. There are dozens of them, all created for different engine types and use purposes. What they all have in common is the letter "W" in the code, sandwiched between some numbers. But what does it mean?
summary: Is your motor oil rated to handle all the conditions your car will experience? You don't need an engineering degree to drive a car, but sometimes it can feel like you need one to buy engine oil for it . Either that or proficiency in some language you don't yet understand.
article_paragraphs: Is your motor oil rated to handle all the conditions your car will experience?

You don't need an engineering degree to drive a car, but sometimes it can feel like you need one to buy engine oil for it . Either that or proficiency in some language you don't yet understand. Because engine oil doesn't just come in one type. There are dozens of them, all created for different engine types and use purposes. What they all have in common is the letter "W" in the code, sandwiched between some numbers. But what does it mean?

The "W" stands for "winter," and when viewed together with the numbers directly preceding it, it tells you how well the oil performs in cold weather conditions. Oil experts call this the winter viscosity grade because it refers to an oil's ability to flow at low temperatures . An oil with a low number before the W, say a 0 or 5, will flow more smoothly when cold than an oil with a higher number, such as 10.

Oil that flows better offers more protection for the engine during the first few seconds of a cold start, when the majority of engine wear occurs. If you live in a region with tough winter weather, your engine has to endure that punishment every day, and possibly multiple times per day. Modern engines with fine tolerances tend to prefer oil with lower W ratings to protect them on startup.

The numbers aren't just plucked out of thin air by oil manufacturers, either. They follow a strict oil viscosity rating system set out by the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE), so you know that oils from different brands will still work in your engine as long as the numbers match the automaker's specification for your car.

Go back to the early days of the car, and oil was marketed as light, medium, or heavy. And even after the oil industry adopted the SAE's number-based rating system in 1926, there was still only one set of numbers printed on an oil can. You can still buy straight SAE 30 or 40 oil today, though it's best reserved for very old cars and machinery.

But this idea of choosing one oil and sticking with it presented a problem, or more accurately an inconvenience. Engineers had realized that a thin oil that prevented wear on startup wasn't so useful when the engine was hot. Because when oil gets warm, it loses some of its viscosity, meaning it gets thinner. And if it gets too thin, it doesn't provide the kind of protective buffer between engine components that's needed to prevent wear. This meant drivers often had to change from a thick summer oil to a thinner winter one when temperatures dropped, and even that solution was a compromise.

This understanding of an engine's different requirements led to the creation of multigrade oils in the 1950s. Multigrades could be thin for cold weather protection, but contained polymers to prevent the oil from getting too thin when warm. They also got a second set of numbers. The first number, the one preceding the letter "W," signals the cold-weather rating, and the second number shows how the oil performs when hot.

title: Red Bull no longer falls away on difficult days: What Austin qualifying reveals about its progress
raw_summary: In Austin, the battle for pole position looked for a long time as though it would be between Max Verstappen and Ferrari . By the end of qualifying, however, the Scuderia had failed to get either car into the top three, while Kimi Antonelli emerged as a surprise contender. Verstappen had to settle for second place, making his conclusion during the Dutch media session in the paddock clear: yes, the Red Bull driver could certainly live with that starting position, but there was still more potential to be unlocked.

article_paragraphs: In Austin, the battle for pole position looked for a long time as though it would be between Max Verstappen and Ferrari . By the end of qualifying, however, the Scuderia had failed to get either car into the top three, while Kimi Antonelli emerged as a surprise contender.

Verstappen had to settle for second place, making his conclusion during the Dutch media session in the paddock clear: yes, the Red Bull driver could certainly live with that starting position, but there was still more potential to be unlocked.

That was especially evident from the Q2 lap with which Verstappen impressed his rivals. On a set of scrubbed tyres, the Dutchman was faster than some drivers from the other top teams on fresh rubber, making a third consecutive pole position seem within reach.

When Autosport asked Verstappen why the picture in Q3 was so different from the second qualifying segment, the four-time world champion explained: "I just didn't have the same grip anymore. It's as simple as that.

"I simply couldn't carry the speed that I wanted through the slow corners anymore. That's something we obviously need to understand, because there was for sure more in it. I just couldn't get it out of the car in Q3."

The wind appears to have been an important factor in that story. In the closing minutes of Q3, many drivers were caught out by gusts of wind, explaining why there were only three improvements on the second runs. Lando Norris spoke of the worst gusts of wind he had ever experienced behind the wheel, which caused him to lock up despite braking earlier as a precaution.
Verstappen clarified, however, that this could not explain the whole story of Q3.

"On the final run, the wind was really bad, but not on the first run. So I don't really understand why it was so disappointing. But anyway, if that's still good enough for second place, then that's okay."

title: Trabant Finally Got A 4-Cylinder Engine Just As East Germans Could Buy Western Cars
raw_summary: After Germany was divided by the U.S. and Russia at the end of World War II, both the Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany) and the German Democratic Republic (East Germany) faced massive industrial rebuilding projects. Both sides needed to get their populations on the move, and both went about it the same way: state-controlled automakers. Volkswagen (which is currently looking at an $18.6 billion restructuring plan ) was in the hands of the German state of Lower Saxony, representing West Germany. Meanwhile, the GDR-owned VEB Sachsenring Automobilewerke Zwickau produced Trabant cars. Trabants wouldn't become quite as popular as VW's rivaling Beetles, but they were successful on their own terms. Despite facing a much smaller market, more than 3 million Trabant vehicles were produced between their launch in 1957 and eventual demise in 1991. They would also get a turn in the cultural spotlight in 1992, when U2 put one on the cover of its album "Achtung, Baby." More recently — and more disturbingly — artist David Černý put a Trabant on legs for his haunting sculpture "Quo Vadis."

Both sides needed to get their populations on the move, and both went about it the same way: state-controlled automakers.
article_paragraphs: After Germany was divided by the U.S. and Russia at the end of World War II, both the Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany) and the German Democratic Republic (East Germany) faced massive industrial rebuilding projects. Both sides needed to get their populations on the move, and both went about it the same way: state-controlled automakers. Volkswagen (which is currently looking at an $18.6 billion restructuring plan ) was in the hands of the German state of Lower Saxony, representing West Germany. Meanwhile, the GDR-owned VEB Sachsenring Automobilewerke Zwickau produced Trabant cars.

Trabants wouldn't become quite as popular as VW's rivaling Beetles, but they were successful on their own terms. Despite facing a much smaller market, more than 3 million Trabant vehicles were produced between their launch in 1957 and eventual demise in 1991. They would also get a turn in the cultural spotlight in 1992, when U2 put one on the cover of its album "Achtung, Baby." More recently — and more disturbingly — artist David Černý put a Trabant on legs for his haunting sculpture "Quo Vadis."

Another way VW's Beetles and Trabant would diverge — for a while — had to do with what was providing motivation. The Beetle famously featured a flat four-stroke, four-cylinder engine right from the start. Trabant relied on two-cylinder, two-stroke mills until 1990 – and when it did switch to a four-cylinder engine, that motor had been licensed from VW. By then, of course, the Berlin Wall was down, Germany was re-united, and Trabant succumbed to stiffer Western competition a year later. Granted, Trabant's dedication to two-cylinder engines wasn't the only thing that held it back, but there were some deeper reasons behind the time it took to modernize its motor.

Given Trabant's original mission of providing affordable transportation, you can understand why its first engines were both two-stroke and two-cylinder. After all, two-stroke motors are usually cheaper and simpler to make than their four-stroke counterparts — although they're also extremely environmentally unfriendly . In terms of cylinder counts, using two instead of four made the process that much cheaper and simpler, too.

Moreover, the typical Trabant didn't need a big engine to do its job. The iconic and long-running 601 — in production for 28 years — was a mere 142 inches long and weighed only 1,400 pounds. It's about the same length as the Chevy Spark, but that car weighed nearly 1,000 pounds more. So, early Trabants didn't need a massive motor to adequately power them. As time went by, however, even the executives recognized the need for a more modern car. But this was where Soviet politics reared its ugly head.

The funds for Trabant development had to be approved by the Soviet Politbüro, but the official in charge simply didn't want to spend the money when the current models were still so popular. Citizens were enduring a 10-year waitlist for them, although how much of that really had to do with their popularity is an open question. That being said, the Politbüro folks actually did make a deal with Volkswagen — as mentioned above — to license VW's 1.1-liter four-stroke engine for Trabant production. But the Berlin Wall had fallen by then, giving people access to Western alternatives. And, as a result, less than 40,000 Trabant 1.1 models would be produced before the model finally went under.

title: Rivian And Volvo Make The Only Large SUVs To Get IIHS Top Safety Pick+ Ratings In 2026
raw_summary: Every year, the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) gives Top Safety Pick and Top Safety Pick+ designations to the new cars that it deems the safest. These selections are determined via crash test results, headlight ratings, pedestrian and vehicle front crash prevention capabilities, seatbelt reminders, ease of child seat lower anchor and tether installation, and whiplash prevention ratings. A Top Safety Pick+ must receive Good ratings in its small and moderate overlap front crash tests, as well as its side tests. Top Safety Pick+ winners also have Acceptable to Good standard headlights, Good standard pedestrian front crash prevention tech, and Acceptable to Good standard vehicle-to-vehicle front crash prevention tech. The organization's website lets you see all its best picks at a glance, and while some segments produce more TSP+ worthy products than others, one that produced a surprisingly small pool was the Large SUV class. Filtering for the biggest of sport utility vehicles that met the IIHS' most stringent requirements, just two made the cut for 2026: the Rivian R1S and the Volvo EX90. They're both electric and are classified as luxury vehicles.

article_paragraphs: Every year, the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) gives Top Safety Pick and Top Safety Pick+ designations to the new cars that it deems the safest. These selections are determined via crash test results, headlight ratings, pedestrian and vehicle front crash prevention capabilities, seatbelt reminders, ease of child seat lower anchor and tether installation, and whiplash prevention ratings. A Top Safety Pick+ must receive Good ratings in its small and moderate overlap front crash tests, as well as its side tests. Top Safety Pick+ winners also have Acceptable to Good standard headlights, Good standard pedestrian front crash prevention tech, and Acceptable to Good standard vehicle-to-vehicle front crash prevention tech.

The organization's website lets you see all its best picks at a glance, and while some segments produce more TSP+ worthy products than others, one that produced a surprisingly small pool was the Large SUV class. Filtering for the biggest of sport utility vehicles that met the IIHS' most stringent requirements, just two made the cut for 2026: the Rivian R1S and the Volvo EX90. They're both electric and are classified as luxury vehicles.

Of the two winners this year, the 2026 Volvo EX90 likely comes as less of a surprise given its brand's extended reputation for safety. Volvo invented the modern three-point seat belt, after all, and gave away the patent to save lives. The EX90 had a bit of a rocky launch last year due to underbaked software, but it's since received a tech overhaul aiming to right those wrongs. In any case, Volvo touts the electric three-row SUV as designed to be "the safest car [it's] ever made," which is a bit like Italy coming out and declaring that one slice of pizza is the most delicious slice it's ever made. In other words, it's probably pretty good.

Safety features include, but aren't limited to, long airbags (referred to as inflatable curtains) that come out of the roofline, front seats designed to protect the spine "during heavy landings," and advanced driver assistance systems that use a combination of cameras, radars, and ultrasonic sensors. The EX90 is offered with a single motor, two motors, or Twin Motor Performance, making 329, 449, and 670 horsepower, respectively. Maximum driving range stands at 305 miles for dual-motor versions, while the single-motor offers 293 miles. The 2026 EX90 starts at $78,090, which includes Volvo's $1,395 destination fee.

Rivian hasn't been around nearly as long as Volvo has. Still, Rivian's R1S predates the EX90, having been released for the 2022 model year (three years before its Volvo counterpart). Updated in 2025 , the three-row, seven-seat electric SUV is one of the few vehicles from a new, non-Tesla American electric car startup that's actually stuck around. Both 2026 and 2027 R1S models are part of the IIHS' latest Top Safety Pick+ list.

The R1S comes standard with cameras and radars that can "learn and predict the behavior of other cars around you." This setup, which facilitates 360-degree perception, includes 10 high-res cameras, five radars, and the ability to "see" 10 seconds ahead. The optional Autonomy+ suite of assisted driving tech is said to allow hands-free driving "wherever there's a painted or dotted line." For 2027, you can get the R1S with either two, three, or four electric motors , with EV range coming in at 410, 371, and 374 miles, respectively. Horsepower figures register at 665 for dual, 850 for tri, and 1,025 for quad. The 2026 R1S lineup also featured a standard battery dual-motor trim with 329 miles of range and 665 horsepower. The entry-level dual-motor 2026 R1S starts at $85,885, which includes the destination charge.

raw_title: Verstappen responds to COTA boss and proposes drastic measures to tackle bumps
title: Verstappen responds to COTA boss and proposes drastic measures to tackle bumps
raw_summary: It is one of the main talking points in the Formula 1 paddock this weekend: the extreme bumps at the Circuit of the Americas. Drivers raised their concerns during Friday evening's drivers' briefing, after which Verstappen stayed behind for some time to speak further with representatives of the FIA and the circuit. Because the track was built on Texas' infamous high-plasticity clay, it suffers from a severe shrink-swell effect. Two years ago, it was completely resurfaced, while two further interventions were carried out ahead of this year's event. The section between Turns 9 and 11 was resurfaced again, while efforts were made to remove the worst bumps between Turns 12 and 19.
summary: It is one of the main talking points in the Formula 1 paddock this weekend: the extreme bumps at the Circuit of the Americas. Drivers raised their concerns during Friday evening's drivers' briefing, after which Verstappen stayed behind for some time to speak further with representatives of the FIA and the circuit.
article_paragraphs: It is one of the main talking points in the Formula 1 paddock this weekend: the extreme bumps at the Circuit of the Americas. Drivers raised their concerns during Friday evening's drivers' briefing, after which Verstappen stayed behind for some time to speak further with representatives of the FIA and the circuit.

Because the track was built on Texas' infamous high-plasticity clay, it suffers from a severe shrink-swell effect. Two years ago, it was completely resurfaced, while two further interventions were carried out ahead of this year's event. The section between Turns 9 and 11 was resurfaced again, while efforts were made to remove the worst bumps between Turns 12 and 19.

According to the drivers, however, that is not enough. Verstappen already described the track conditions as "unacceptable" and "out of control" on Thursday, adding on Saturday that he is taking painkillers every day in Austin, just as Lando Norris needs headache tablets for every session.
When the bumps came up again after qualifying during Verstappen’s Dutch media round in the paddock, he said: "There are a few corners here that are simply really unacceptable."

That appears to refer primarily to the enormous bump under braking for Turn 1 and a rather dangerous one at Turn 19, but when Autosport put that to Verstappen, he explained that there are more problem areas.

"Turns 1 and 19 are indeed really bad, but also that whole fast section between Turns 4 and 5, there are such big bumps there... Of course I understand that the ground here is a problem, but that's something you should have looked at beforehand. That really shouldn't be an excuse."

Besides placing considerable physical strain on the drivers, the bumps through the Esses are also potentially dangerous. Several drivers have already come close to losing control of their cars at that point during the practice sessions in Austin, and if things actually go wrong through the sequence of high-speed corners, the consequences could be immense.
"Yes, those are things that really shouldn't happen at such high speeds, when the car bottoms out like that", Verstappen said.

Combined, those things probably mean that your next lawn mower is more likely to plug in than fill up, whether you like it or not. The good news is that. in addition to being quieter, safer, and not poisoning the air you breathe while you walk behind them , electric laenmowers have come a long way in terms of power and performance in just a few years. So much so, in fact, that many of the highest-rated models on Amazon, emphatic period , are electric.

In putting this list together, we looked at the average star ratings of a number of lawn mowers on Amazon, focusing on products that had at least 2,000 reviews and a four-star average or higher, and found that (like last year) battery-electric units from EGO Power, Greenworks, and Worx were among the top-rated mowers, regardless of fuel type.

Over the past few years, the EGO POWER+ brand has staked a claim to being the gold standard for cordless lawn equipment, thanks to its high-voltage 56V battery platform and premium build quality. The brand’s 21″ POWER+ LM2112 push mower currently carries a 4.5-star average rating from more than 2,200 Amazon reviews and an “Overall Pick” designation .

That’s no surprise, given the LM2112’s 6 ft-lbs. of cutting torque (equivalent to a 150cc ICE), and up to 35 minutes of runtime (call it a suburban yard) from the included 56V 4.0 Ah li-ion battery , three-in-one mulching, bagging and side-discharge capability. It also starts at the push of a button, folds for compact storage and skips the exhaust, maintenance, and oil changes that come along with a comparable gas mower.

With an impressive 4.2-star rating after more than 12,000 verified reviews, the Greenworks 40V 16″ push mower is in rare company among mowers of any kind on Amazon . No surprise, given that the lightweight, cordless mower weighs just 37.5 lbs. and comes with a 4.0Ah battery and charger good for up to 40 minutes of runtime, making it ideal for homeowners with smaller yards who want to ditch gas without wrestling with a heavier machine.

The Greenpower’s 16″ cutting deck is designed for (if not limited to) compact lawns, with a five-position height adjustment and a two-in-one system offering you a choice of mulching (yes) or bagging (no) your lawn clippings.

For bigger, more demanding lawns, Greenworks offers a 4.4-star push mower with a 21″ steel cutting deck that’s powered by an 80V brushless motor and ships with a pair of 2.0 Ah batteries good for up to 40 minutes of runtime with both batteries . Three-in-one functionality for mulching, bagging, or side discharge is included, too, along with push-button starting, seven-position height adjustment, and a rapid charger that can get it back to work in about 30 minutes.

title: Police pull over two men riding an electric couch down the street
raw_summary: Electric scooters have carried just about everything at this point, from commuters and tourists to groceries and probably more than a few ill-advised passengers. But two riders in Charlotte, North Carolina, may have just raised the bar after police stopped them cruising down the street on an actual couch apparently powered by a pair of Lime electric scooters. Officers with the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department encountered the unusual contraption traveling down South Tryon Street, according to a recent post shared by the department.

But two riders in Charlotte, North Carolina, may have just raised the bar after police stopped them cruising down the street on an actual couch apparently powered by a pair of Lime electric scooters.
article_paragraphs: Electric scooters have carried just about everything at this point, from commuters and tourists to groceries and probably more than a few ill-advised passengers. But two riders in Charlotte, North Carolina, may have just raised the bar after police stopped them cruising down the street on an actual couch apparently powered by a pair of Lime electric scooters.
Officers with the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department encountered the unusual contraption traveling down South Tryon Street, according to a recent post shared by the department.

“Well, this was certainly a first,” police wrote. “Our EDU Officers encountered quite the situation this weekend when they stopped two gentlemen traveling down S. Tryon Street on a couch… Yes, an actual couch.”

From the photo, the setup appears to consist of a full-size sofa perched across two Lime shared electric scooters. Exactly how the scooters were attached – or how steering was accomplished – isn’t clear. But judging by the fact that the riders apparently made it far enough to attract police attention, the system seems to have worked at least reasonably well with some coordinated efforts by the dual pilots.
And frankly, as someone who has famously seen and operated plenty of bizarre electric vehicles over the years, I have to give some points for creativity here.
Police seemed to feel similarly, though they were understandably less enthusiastic about the safety implications of piloting living-room furniture down a public street.
“While we appreciate the creativity, we do have to remind everyone: no matter what you’re ‘driving’ (using that term extremely loosely), please think about safety first,” the department wrote.
Police also joked that it was “probably best to leave the mobile furniture displays to IKEA.”

raw_title: MotoGP's final Phillip Island race cancelled, replaced with parade lap
title: MotoGP's final Phillip Island race cancelled, replaced with parade lap
raw_summary: The 2026 Australian Grand Prix MotoGP race at Phillip Island has been cancelled due to adverse weather conditions. "Poor visibility affecting the operation of the medical helicopter" meant the day's planned track action in any of the three classes of grand prix racing never got underway - as there was never a sufficient break in the weather to even attempt racing. MotoGP first cancelled the Moto3 race, then the Moto2 race, then finally called off the premier-class event at 3.35pm local time - having accepted that the hope to get the race started at 4.30pm was in vain. In lieu of the race, MotoGP riders "will do a lap behind the safety car and stop on the main straight to greet the fans". This will function as a "farewell lap" to the Phillip Island venue, which will be replaced as the host of the Australian GP next year by the street track in Adelaide. "To every fan who came to Phillip Island today, despite the conditions, thank you. Your support is a powerful reminder of the love for MotoGP and the special place Phillip Island holds in Australian motorsport," they said in a statement.

"While this is not the way anyone wanted MotoGP's time at Phillip Island to conclude, it does not diminish the incredible legacy of this event. We thank the fans, riders, teams, officials, volunteers, partners and the Phillip Island community who have made it so special over so many years." The premier class, MotoGP, at least exits Phillip Island having contested a sprint race in the dry. Moto3 and Moto2 fields will leave without having raced, after logging a respective 1446 laps and 1500 laps across practice and qualifying on the two previous days. Sunday had long been anticipated to offer the worst of the weather this weekend - but MotoGP did not pursue a repeat of its 2023 strategy, when it successfully ran the full-distance grand prix on Saturday and then scheduled the sprint on Sunday (and subsequently cancelled it). Championship leader Marc Marquez leaves Phillip Island with a 10-point cushion over Jorge Martin with a scheduled four rounds left (as question marks remain over the Qatar Grand Prix). The Sunday cancellation is a massive reprieve for the injured Martin, who it is thought will attempt to compete next weekend at Sepang.

raw_summary: We've looked at five features that make police cars different from their civilian counterparts, and concluded they don't really get better engines . Yet as the Michigan State Police found out this fall, those motors can still be impressively effective. Their testing was part of an annual program that dates back to 1975 and over the years has become an industry benchmark. This time around, 13 cars — and five motorcycles — were put through their paces on two separate courses. Chelsea Proving Ground, located in Chelsea, MI., and owned by Stellantis, was used to evaluate the vehicles' top speed, acceleration, and braking. Vehicle dynamics were tested at Grattan Raceway in Belding, MI. Incidentally, the historic Grattan track was for sale when this article was written, with a listing price of a cool $15 million.
