article_paragraphs: We've looked at five features that make police cars different from their civilian counterparts, and concluded they don't really get better engines . Yet as the Michigan State Police found out this fall, those motors can still be impressively effective. Their testing was part of an annual program that dates back to 1975 and over the years has become an industry benchmark.

This time around, 13 cars — and five motorcycles — were put through their paces on two separate courses. Chelsea Proving Ground, located in Chelsea, MI., and owned by Stellantis, was used to evaluate the vehicles' top speed, acceleration, and braking. Vehicle dynamics were tested at Grattan Raceway in Belding, MI. Incidentally, the historic Grattan track was for sale when this article was written, with a listing price of a cool $15 million.

As for the fastest, that was the all-wheel-drive Ford Police Interceptor Utility. It leveraged its 3.0-liter EcoBoost V6 — making 400 horsepower and 415 pound-feet of torque – to hit an electronically limited 148 mph. That was faster than the faster police motorcycle, too. On the two-wheeled side of the ledger, the leader was the BMW R 1300 RT-P in its standard setup — with a maximum velocity of 141 mph that was again electronically limited. In fact, all the vehicles in the test had top speeds limited by manufacturers.

The results are nothing new, though. The Blue Oval's Interceptor Utility has been the fastest car in the Michigan State Police ranks since it shared that honor with the Dodge Charger back in 2020. Rounding out the 2026 top 6 for top speed were the AWD Ford Police Interceptor with hybrid and gas-only powertrains, both listed at 136 mph, and the RWD Chevrolet Tahoe PPV with the 5.3-liter V8, the Chevrolet Blazer PPV EV with AWD, and the Dodge Durango Pursuit with a 5.7-liter V8 and AWD. That trio clocked in at 130 mph.

Of course, top speed is only one important criteria for police performance, so the MSP went on to measure the vehicles' 0 – 60 sprint times — even though tracking a car going from 5 – 60 is usually a superior performance metric . Anyways, results here went about the way you might have expected once you realized not one but two EVs were on the test roster. The nearly instant torque delivered by the Blazer EV and the AWD Ford Mustang Mach-E GT helped them set the bar for acceleration: The former measured at 5.14 seconds and the latter leading the way at a brisk 4.03 seconds.

Ford's PIU with the 3.0-liter EcoBoost and the Ford F-150 Police Responder, which upsizes to a 3.5-liter EcoBoost mill, are the only other non-motorcycles to get in under 6 seconds. The quickest police cars with internal combustion engines did the job in 5.95 and 5.68 seconds, respectively. The quickest motorcycle, the BMW 1300 R-PT with the Dynamic Pack and AutoShift, was then the only vehicle to break the 4.0-second mark. It finished the sprint in only 3.61 seconds.

It's also worth pointing out that the MSP checked 0-to-100 times, with pretty much the same results. The quickest EV was again the Mach-E, the two quickest gas-powered cars were the Ford PIU and F-150 Police Responder, and the quickest bike was the BMW with the Dynamic Pack/AutoShift.

Considering how dangerous high-speed pursuits are , a good set of stoppers and superior vehicle dynamics are vital for police vehicles as well. With that in mind, the MSP put its test vehicles through multiple "60 – 0 mph full ABS maximum deceleration stops" to come up with a final projected stopping distance from that speed. The Mustang Mach-E came out on top in this testing, bolstered by a projected stopping distance of 122.45 feet. No other vehicle tested was below 130 feet. Moreover, one pass with the Mach-E saw the car go from 59.7 mph to a complete halt in 116.75 feet. Meanwhile, the MSP's fastest police vehicle — the Ford PIU with the 3.0-liter EcoBoost — had the seventh-shortest stopping-distance projection, at 137.24 feet. The 2026 Ram 2500, with four-wheel drive and a 6.4-liter V8, provides some context with a projected stopping distance of 170.13 feet that was by far the longest in the MSP testing.

Their testing was part of an annual program that dates back to 1975 and over the years has become an industry benchmark.

Ford unveiled the Econoline van in September of 1960 as a 1961 model, and amazingly, the vans remained in production over four generations until 2014, the cutaway and stripped-chassis versions that sit under ambulances, shuttle buses, and Class C motorhomes are still being built however. A remarkable 65 years of continuous production.
Ford unveiled the Econoline van in September of 1960 as a 1961 model, and amazingly, the vans remained in production over four generations until 2014. Image courtesy of Ford.
Volkswagen started a van-arms race of sorts among the larger US manufacturers. The VW Type 2 van sold surprisingly well in the United States in the late 1950s, and Detroit certainly noticed.

The Chevrolet team even went so far as to copy the air-cooled, rear-engined layout for its Corvair 95 van . Ford, which began development of their own van series in 1957, went another way entirely. The blue oval engineers took the drivetrain from its new Falcon compact car, built a unit-construction van body around it on a 90 inch wheelbase, and put the engine under a cover between the two front seats, with the driver sitting above the front axle.

A 144 cubic inch (2.4 liter) six was the standard engine, and it came with solid axles on leaf springs at both ends. The Econoline replaced Ford’s F-Series panel delivery series and it came as a delivery van, a station bus, and in a pickup variant.

Ford expected the pickup to be the stronger seller than it actually was, but buyers weren’t that interested in it. Of the 544,335 Econolines built in the United States through to 1967, just 52,121 were pickups, and the body style ended with the first generation. This is perhaps not all that surprising, given that Ford (and the American market overall) already had plenty of fully-fledged pickup trucks in production at the time that made more sense for cargo hauling.

title: How Verstappen lost pole to Antonelli
raw_summary: Either Red Bull driver could have been on pole position for Formula 1’s United States Grand Prix were they not thwarted by Kimi Antonelli turning the tables through a crucial sequence of corners. An intense qualifying fight came down to Antonelli versus Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar in Q3, and especially their opening runs - on which the Mercedes and the Red Bull traded dominance across the lap.

Sunday is Antonelli’s first chance to wrap up the world championship. It’s a mathematical long shot but he is in the best place to do it after a qualifying lap worthy of the cause.

Antonelli was superb through the latter part of the sweeps in the opening sector. The deeper into that sequence, the more assured he looked, throwing the car into each part with precise aggression even as the engine cried loudly with Antonelli holding it in a lower gear versus Verstappen.

Antonelli used it to carry prodigious speed holding the throttle for longer into Turn 7, rolling that through Turn 8 and picking up the throttle more aggressively into Turn 9, gaining almost two tenths through these corners versus the Red Bull.
“Medium-speed corners, high-speed, medium-speed,” Antonelli said of where the lap was sweetest.
“It felt in a good place, the car. We still struggle a little bit in low speed, but overall the car has been very good in Sector 1 and Sector 2, especially through Turns 8 and 9.
“So that's where we feel the most gain from the package. It's still the low speed that we're trying to understand.”

raw_title: The two weaknesses conspiring against Ferrari at Austin
title: The two weaknesses conspiring against Ferrari at Austin
raw_summary: Friday Formula 1 pacesetter Ferrari fell short of a grand prix pole position for the 18th time in 2026, this time at Austin, because of two familiar weaknesses and unfortunate timing. Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton ended up fourth and fifth but had slightly different views on why they could not match Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes and the two Red Bulls.

Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton ended up fourth and fifth but had slightly different views on why they could not match Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes and the two Red Bulls.
article_paragraphs: Friday Formula 1 pacesetter Ferrari fell short of a grand prix pole position for the 18th time in 2026, this time at Austin, because of two familiar weaknesses and unfortunate timing.
Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton ended up fourth and fifth but had slightly different views on why they could not match Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes and the two Red Bulls.
This year's Ferrari has battled a single-lap tyre weakness that has left it weaker on Saturdays than Sundays for much of the year.

"It's very disappointing because I think there are some other weekends where we've been strong in free practice, but then come quali, it's very clear that the others are just having a lot more in the straights, and it's very difficult for us to match that," Friday pacesetter Leclerc said.
"But I felt like it's a qualifying where we had the potential in the car, but the car also includes tyres, and in Q3, unfortunately, we were not in the right place.
"It was like 1°C or 2°C less in Q3, and for me, it was a huge difference. Just really struggled in the outlap.
"I was sliding quite a lot already from the outlap, and that made it very difficult after that."
Leclerc called on Ferrari to "work harder and try and understand those tyres very well, even better than what we are doing now, because the others I think normally have a bit more".

raw_title: Why Pickup Trucks Are Traditionally Chosen Over SUVs For Big Towing Jobs
title: Why Pickup Trucks Are Traditionally Chosen Over SUVs For Big Towing Jobs
raw_summary: America loves trucks. Whether it's a horse trailer or a 30-foot camper, somebody somewhere in the U.S. is hooking it to a pickup right now. On the surface, a full-size truck and a big SUV look cut from the same cloth: both are built for utility, both sit high, and both can pull a trailer. So why are pickups still chosen for big towing jobs? The short answer: pickups are designed to tow more, and the proof shows up even when a truck and an SUV share the same bones. J.D. Power notes the Chevrolet Tahoe is "built on the same platform as the Chevrolet Silverado 1500 pickup," yet the 2026 Tahoe tops out at 8,400 pounds while the Silverado 1500 is rated for 13,300 pounds. Ford's lineup tells the same story, with the 2026 Expedition maxing out at 9,600 pounds and the 2026 F-150 at 13,500 pounds. SUVs can tow, but they reach their limits sooner, and Consumer Reports warns against towing "at or near your vehicle's capacity."

article_paragraphs: America loves trucks. Whether it's a horse trailer or a 30-foot camper, somebody somewhere in the U.S. is hooking it to a pickup right now. On the surface, a full-size truck and a big SUV look cut from the same cloth: both are built for utility, both sit high, and both can pull a trailer. So why are pickups still chosen for big towing jobs?

The short answer: pickups are designed to tow more, and the proof shows up even when a truck and an SUV share the same bones. J.D. Power notes the Chevrolet Tahoe is "built on the same platform as the Chevrolet Silverado 1500 pickup," yet the 2026 Tahoe tops out at 8,400 pounds while the Silverado 1500 is rated for 13,300 pounds. Ford's lineup tells the same story, with the 2026 Expedition maxing out at 9,600 pounds and the 2026 F-150 at 13,500 pounds. SUVs can tow, but they reach their limits sooner, and Consumer Reports warns against towing "at or near your vehicle's capacity."

In heavy-duty territory, the gap becomes a canyon. With Ford's High-Capacity Gooseneck Tow Package, a 2026 F-450 is rated to pull 40,000 pounds, a figure even new SUVs with impressive towing capacities can't come close to. (The Jeep Grand Wagoneer leads the full-size SUV class at 10,000 pounds, which still leaves it behind most full-size pickups.)

Truck beds almost never connect to the cab — the two sit on a heavy frame as separate pieces, since a one-piece body would be too stiff to take the twisting that comes with heavy towing. Most SUVs skip that setup. Take Ford's Explorer, a unibody midsize three-row SUV: it's rated to tow 5,000 pounds, less than half of what an F-150 can pull.

Out back, the classic utilitarian pickup recipe calls for leaf springs. It's old-school hardware, and it's stuck around on trucks because it's the better fit for heavy towing. The trade-off is comfort. Most SUVs ride on coil springs, which give passengers a softer ride but aren't usually set up for big towing jobs. Then there's where the weight sits. As The RV Geeks explain, "a truck can carry more weight positioned right above its rear axle," which is where gooseneck and fifth-wheel hitches go.

Ford's Super Duty ratings show the payoff, with the max rating dropping by 10,000 pounds when you swap a gooseneck for a conventional hitch. Trucks tend to offer more specialized towing equipment such as towing mirrors, trailer brake controllers, specialized axle ratios, and heavy-duty cooling systems. They also tend to have a longer wheelbase compared to a comparably sized SUV – this can be a problem in tight parking spots and crowded city streets, but it helps with stability while towing.

Lastly, there's the engine. Heavy-duty trucks offer big diesels, and the Super Duty's top option makes up to 1,200 lb-ft of torque — not something you can get in an SUV. Put it all together and a pickup isn't just stronger on paper; it's built around the trailer from the frame up.

In terms of people-hauling, six is the ceiling for a full-size pickup. Big SUVs play a different game. The 2026 Chevy Suburban seats up to nine, and third-row riders get 36.7 inches of legroom. Try fitting a carpool into a crew cab. No pickup offers a third row, so the soccer team is out of luck. Size down to the Honda Pilot, and you can still get up to eight seats.

article_paragraphs: What looked like a wide open Formula 1 qualifying session at the United States Grand Prix - or perhaps even one where Ferrari was clear favourite - somehow ended up with the runaway championship leader on pole.
Which means plenty of disappointed people in our winners and losers selection.

Yet again in 2026, Ferrari falters when it actually counts. That clean sweep of fastest practice times looked so convincing, and yet given it's this team, there was still that element of doubt. Would Ferrari and/or its drivers somehow fumble qualifying? Would something go tactically wrong?
In the end, it just wasn't quick enough in qualifying trim - rivals able to exploit deployment possibilities much better, and Charles Leclerc ruing poor tyre prep too.
And this doesn't seem like a case where qualifying will be the blip and there's loads of untapped race pace in store for Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton to charge forward with.
This Ferrari might just be better at looking quick in the sessions that don't actually matter. - Matt Beer

In the weeks where his coronation as a remarkably young F1 world champion has looked ever more secure, Antonelli has actually been keeping a relatively low profile on track, unable to work his usual magic amid the confusion around Mercedes' upgrade.
So despite the fact he's on the cusp of sealing the title with multiple (who really knows how many) races to spare, Antonelli's pole here feels slightly out of the blue.

raw_title: Public Beaches In Texas Are Also Highways, And You Can Actually Drive On Them
title: Public Beaches In Texas Are Also Highways, And You Can Actually Drive On Them
raw_summary: There's something special about driving down a beach; the slight squeak of sand under your tires, the murmur of the crashing waves, the feel of your vehicle working just a little bit harder, all make you feel like part of the beautiful wild scenery. The early sand racers of Daytona knew the feeling. The 1960's dune buggy culture of Southern California made driving on beaches even cooler. In Texas, drivers embrace beaches in a big way, enjoying over 200 miles of drivable beaches. Texans so enjoy their access to beaches that they coded public access into state law in 1959 with the Open Beaches Act. In 2009, Texans voted with a 76.9% approval rate to add it to the state constitution. Essentially, the area from the low tide line to the line of continuous vegetation is public domain that can not be impeded. The Texas General Land Office is charged with enforcing the Act, and local jurisdictions have some say on what "public access" means to them. article_paragraphs: There's something special about driving down a beach; the slight squeak of sand under your tires, the murmur of the crashing waves, the feel of your vehicle working just a little bit harder, all make you feel like part of the beautiful wild scenery. The early sand racers of Daytona knew the feeling. The 1960's dune buggy culture of Southern California made driving on beaches even cooler. In Texas, drivers embrace beaches in a big way, enjoying over 200 miles of drivable beaches.

Texans so enjoy their access to beaches that they coded public access into state law in 1959 with the Open Beaches Act. In 2009, Texans voted with a 76.9% approval rate to add it to the state constitution. Essentially, the area from the low tide line to the line of continuous vegetation is public domain that can not be impeded. The Texas General Land Office is charged with enforcing the Act, and local jurisdictions have some say on what "public access" means to them. There are stipulations such as public safety needs or environmental concerns, for example, which allows a municipality to restrict driving on beaches.

Despite some restrictions, there are a lot of beaches to choose from . Every beach is considered a Texas State Highway, so all traffic laws apply – yes including seatbelts. Flip flops and bare feet are legally allowed. Also, like some highways, you may have to pay to play, as a majority of the beaches have some sort of access fee. Surfside Beach is on the pricey side at $15 daily, while that $15 will get you a year of access and maybe a hot dog or two at Matagorda Beach. Make delicious choices.

There are a handful of free beaches as well. For those into SpaceX, Boca Chica Beach may be the spot for you. Closer to Galveston, the West End beaches offer free access to beaches. The vibe of the beaches varies wildly. Beaches closer to bigger cities can seem like little more than sandy parking lots, but with a little bit of work you can find more solitude.For true privacy, Texas has the "Longest Undeveloped Beach Drive in the World." The Padre Island National Seashore offers 66 miles of beach adventure. This is a wild beach with soft sand and other obstacles, so a four-wheel-drive vehicle is your best bet. There are no services, so come prepared with food, beverages, gas and probably recovery gear. For your efforts, you'll be rewarded with beautiful scenery, plenty of wildlife and a good bit of peace and quiet. Bring a tent and fishing pole and make a couple days out of it!

If you're sold on beach driving, but not actively in Texas, don't fret big fella. There are plenty of places nationwide to get your fix. We mentioned California's dune buggy culture earlier. The "birthplace" of that culture, Oceano Dunes State Vehicular Recreation Area in Southern California just reopened for your driving pleasure. Further north on the west coast, Washington has a 28-mile run out on Long Beach Peninsula. On the east coast, "heading down the Cape" of Cape Cod is a popular summer pastime . Further south, Cape Hatteras National Seashore has over 50 miles of accessible beach, including Corolla Beach, which has wild horses just wandering around, being wild. Go eve further south to Florida and there is, of course, Daytona Beach. Nearby, venture to lesser known New Smyrna Beach, where this writer cut his teeth driving the beach in a beat up old Chevette.

article_paragraphs: Born in Germany in the late 1870s, the Duesenberg brothers — Frederick (Fred) and August (Augie) – would move to America and make some of the time's most luxurious and innovative cars. One of their earliest ventures included opening a garage in Iowa circa 1903 – which is where they landed after immigrating. During this time, Fred and August were modifying and racing cars.

Now, we're skipping a lot of steps here, but after gaining a reputation as brilliant engineers — and developing motors for the military during World War I – the brothers found themselves in New Jersey. The Garden State proved to be fertile soil for the two, as that's where the first Duesenberg straight-8 engine was created.

Straight-8 power became a defining characteristic of Duesenberg race cars, which in turn became some of the era's most dominant performers. They not only won at Indy — claiming the checkered flag three times during the 1920s — but also at Le Mans.

Le Mans was where Jimmy Murphy ran away from the field, winning by about 14 minutes over heavily favored early motorsports pioneer Ralph DePalma. Just keep in mind we're talking about the 1921 French Grand Prix here, not the 24-hour endurance race used by the likes of Michelin to refine its tire designs .

A key Le Mans advantage for the Duesenbergs was that their latest cars now sported four-wheel hydraulic brakes. Fred would file patents for his four-wheel hydraulic-brake setup in 1920, with the system being deployed for the brothers' first passenger car a year later. This development made the 1921 Duesenberg Model A the first production car with that particular technology.

While the Duesenberg Model A was the first production-series vehicle with four-wheel hydraulic brakes, the brothers couldn't claim they invented the technology. Let's take a closer look at what preceded the Model A's brakes and how these events influenced the system's design.

The first solid evidence of four-wheel mechanical brakes comes with the 1912 Argyll 15 HP, with a system developed by Henri Perrot. The French engineer would earn the first U.S. patent for a four-wheel mechanical brake system in 1913 while working for Argyll.

Next, sources credit a company called Knox Motors with offering a form of hydraulic brakes on the rear wheels of its commercial trucks as early as 1915. Little known today, Knox also built one of the world's first motorized fire trucks.

title: Martin injury update hints at early racing return bid
raw_summary: MotoGP championship contender Jorge Martin may be targeting a sooner than expected return to race action after the Phillip Island injury that seemed to have ended his title shot. Martin’s Aprilia team announced on Sunday morning that Martin will remain in Australia this week despite breaking his arm on Saturday during the sprint race.
summary: MotoGP championship contender Jorge Martin may be targeting a sooner than expected return to race action after the Phillip Island injury that seemed to have ended his title shot. Martin’s Aprilia team announced on Sunday morning that Martin will remain in Australia this week despite breaking his arm on Saturday during the sprint race.
article_paragraphs: MotoGP championship contender Jorge Martin may be targeting a sooner than expected return to race action after the Phillip Island injury that seemed to have ended his title shot.
Martin’s Aprilia team announced on Sunday morning that Martin will remain in Australia this week despite breaking his arm on Saturday during the sprint race.
That potentially opens the door for an attempted return at Sepang in one week’s time.

Initial reports from the team on Saturday afternoon suggested that Martin had broken both the radius and ulna in his right arm, but said that he would first travel to hospital in Melbourne (two hours away from the Phillip Island track) for further assessment.
That assessment turned out to be good news, with a suspected fracture of his ulna (the smaller bone in the lower arm) ruled out.
“Jorge Martin underwent a CT scan to assess his condition following yesterday’s injury. The only confirmed injury is a non-displaced fracture of the distal radius,” said Aprilia’s statement.
“Consequently, the rider will not be returning to Spain and will undergo the necessary treatment over the coming days.”

With MotoGP travelling directly from Australia to Malaysia for the next of its back-to-back races at Sepang, the news that Martin will not go back home but will instead remain in the region very much opens the door for an attempt to return next weekend.

summary: Volkswagen is offering its Chinese-market Jetta M6 electric sedan with nearly 290 miles of CLTC-rated range for less than $12,000 (USD), and if that’s not what “der people’s wagen” should be all about, I don’t know what is.
article_paragraphs: Volkswagen is offering its Chinese-market Jetta M6 electric sedan with nearly 290 miles of CLTC-rated range for less than $12,000 (USD), and if that’s not what “der people’s wagen” should be all about, I don’t know what is.

Launched as a joint venture between FAW and Volkswagen Group, the Jetta brand’s first battery electric car is finally here – and it is a genuinely accessible , capable , and kinda decent-looking family sedan in the same way VW’s original Type I was when it was first developed in the 1940s.

The new Jetta M6 was launched earlier this in three variants: the 465 Pro, 555 Max and 555 Ultra; each priced at 79,800 yuan (~$11,800), 89,800 yuan and 99,800 yuan, respectively, with the model numbers corresponding to the car’s estimated CLTC range in kilometers (which maths out around ~285 and 345 miles, if you’re curious).

Built on FAW’s Jiesi architecture , the M6 measures 4,806 mm long and 1,868 mm wide, putting it right in that sedan sweet spot between the Civic/Corolla and Accord/Camry crews, and within a few mm this way and that of the Tesla Model 3, so it should have plenty of room for young professionals and families – but the M6′ real selling point is its tech.

Inside, the Jetta M6 offers an 8.88″ driver display along with a big 15.6″ central touchscreen that integrates Chinese AI assistants Doubao and DeepSeek and ships with Apple CarPlay baked in. Advanced ADAS with , “intelligent cruise assistance, automatic emergency braking, and automated parking” is standard.

The entry-level “465 Pro” version of the Jetta M6 comes equipped with 42.9 kWh LFP battery and a 113 kW (~150 hp) electric motor driving the front wheels, a combination the company says is good for a 8.3-second sprint to 100 km/h (62 mph). Stepping up to the 555 versions gets you a larger 51.9 kWh battery and more powerful 145 kW (~195 hp) motor that cuts that sprint to 6.8 seconds.
Both the 42.9 and 51.0 kWh batteries are lithium iron phosphate deals supplied by CALB, with charging from 20% to 80% taking about 30 minutes.

Would those features and performance numbers be enough to get you to look at something like this in the US, even at twice the price? It seems to me that North America’s VW dealers need all the help they can get, and a volume leader like this with a “back to basics” ad campaign that plays on a different kind of nostalgia – nostalgia for a time when people could afford a Jetta , maybe? – could be a winner. Let us know what you think in the comments.

title: Antonelli on US GP pole as Ferrari challenge falls apart
raw_summary: Formula 1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli beat Max Verstappen to pole position for the United States Grand Prix as practice pacesetter Ferrari watched its challenge crumble in qualifying. Antonelli came good as the qualifying hour went on and beat Verstappen by 0.179s in Q3 to clinch his seventh pole position of the season, while Isack Hadjar made it two Red Bulls in the top three.
summary: Formula 1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli beat Max Verstappen to pole position for the United States Grand Prix as practice pacesetter Ferrari watched its challenge crumble in qualifying. Antonelli came good as the qualifying hour went on and beat Verstappen by 0.179s in Q3 to clinch his seventh pole position of the season, while Isack Hadjar made it two Red Bulls in the top three.
article_paragraphs: Formula 1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli beat Max Verstappen to pole position for the United States Grand Prix as practice pacesetter Ferrari watched its challenge crumble in qualifying.
Antonelli came good as the qualifying hour went on and beat Verstappen by 0.179s in Q3 to clinch his seventh pole position of the season, while Isack Hadjar made it two Red Bulls in the top three.

Antonelli was one of three drivers - alongside Mercedes team-mate George Russell and the McLaren of Oscar Piastri - to go through Q1 on mediums in order to save an extra set of soft tyres for Q3. (Something Red Bull did too by running Verstappen and Hadjar on one set of softs in Q1 and Q2.)
Having been sixth in Q1, Antonelli then ended Q2 just 0.080s off the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc at the top of the Q2 order, and jumped to provisional pole at the start of Q3 with a 1m34.035s.

He had been more than a tenth up on that time through the second sector on his final attempt, but then had a big correction on the exit of the Turn 13 right-hander that wrecked that attempt and appeared to open the door to his rivals.

But the Red Bulls failed to improve their times - both actually had their final, slower efforts scrubbed off for track-limits offences - and with Leclerc finding less than a tenth, that meant Antonelli held on to pole.
Verstappen said in failing to beat Antonelli that, having come through Q1 and Q2 on the same set of tyres, "for whatever reason on both of those sets [in Q3] I didn't have a good balance".
Third for Hadjar marked a drastic turnaround for the second Red Bull driver after struggling throughout practice, as Ferrari's fortunes went the other way.

raw_title: 6 WD-40 Myths Gearheads Need To Stop Believing
title: 6 WD-40 Myths Gearheads Need To Stop Believing
raw_summary: If someone came to you selling a product with an incredible range of uses made from a secret formula first tested on missiles, you might think it's BS. However, this progression represents WD-40's actual origin. WD-40 was created by the Rocket Chemical Company, which was founded in 1953 by Norm Larsen. Three Rocket Chemical staff members achieved the product's formula after 40 trials, which is naturally where the name WD-40 comes from. What goes into the formula is considered a trade secret, like the recipe for Coca-Cola, Kentucky Fried Chicken, or the Tesla FSD data snagged by Dutch regulators . Furthermore, trade secrets don't expire the way patents do. Aerospace contractor Convair initially used WD-40 on its Atlas Missile (America's first successful intercontinental ballistic missile) to protect against rust and corrosion.

article_paragraphs: If someone came to you selling a product with an incredible range of uses made from a secret formula first tested on missiles, you might think it's BS. However, this progression represents WD-40's actual origin.

WD-40 was created by the Rocket Chemical Company, which was founded in 1953 by Norm Larsen. Three Rocket Chemical staff members achieved the product's formula after 40 trials, which is naturally where the name WD-40 comes from. What goes into the formula is considered a trade secret, like the recipe for Coca-Cola, Kentucky Fried Chicken, or the Tesla FSD data snagged by Dutch regulators . Furthermore, trade secrets don't expire the way patents do. Aerospace contractor Convair initially used WD-40 on its Atlas Missile (America's first successful intercontinental ballistic missile) to protect against rust and corrosion.
When discussing WD-40, it's important to recognize the range of stories that aren't true. Below are six WD-40 myths that continue circulating, some of which are downright baffling.

If you've been reading Jalopnik recently, you'll know this one isn't true. Right off the bat, you shouldn't use it on your wiper blades ; it's terrible for squeaky engine belts , and it can lead to some entertaining damage if you replace your engine oil with the stuff .

Part of the misconception has to do with WD-40's lubricating properties. The company itself says that the Multi-Use Product is "a unique, special blend of lubricants" that works to keep your car's door hinges and hood latches moving free and easy. It's just that the experts don't always agree. Yes, WD-40 may help in the short term, but it will quickly evaporate and, in some cases, clean off and dry up the original factory grease.

On the other hand, WD-40 is still too slippery to spray on your brake components, and that's no matter how squeaky they sound. Moreover, that noise could be telling you it's time for new brakes, anyway.

Just remember that we're talking about WD-40's traditional Multi-Use Product here. The company has a full family of WD-40 products that can pick up the slack where the regular stuff isn't up for the job. To properly lubricate parts long-term, like those door hinges, for instance, the company makes WD-40 White Lithium Grease.
Since WD-40 has some lubricating properties, some might think it could do the same for your joints. While many know it cannot, we'll still explore where this ridiculous misconception can stem from.

This week, Canada and the EU both backed away from their existing commitments to reduce motor vehicle emissions. Oh, they still promise to get around to it, just not now, while political turmoil is roiling their economies. The promises will be kept — make no mistake about that — just not now. They need breathing room to attend to the high prices resulting from America’s failed effort to wipe Iran off the map and to address extreme right wing movements who threaten to bring down their governments. There are always plenty of reasons to delay, delay, and delay some more.

According to Canadian website Electric Autonomy , the government of Canada this week announced a freeze on its vehicle emissions mandates for three years, while promising to still reach its goal of 75 percent of new car sales to be electric by 2035. That and three loonies will get you a doughnut at Tim Horton’s.

The current standard is 172 grams of greenhouse gas emissions per mile (107 grams/km) and it will remain at the level now through the end of 2029. Thereafter, God willing and the creek don’t rise, the standard will begin ratcheting down every year until it reaches 74 grams per mile (46 grams/km).

A joint release by prime minister Mark Carney and Ontario premier Doug Ford said, “Maintaining the fleet average performance standard will provide manufacturers with near-term flexibility at a time when the industry is facing trade-related pressures. It will also provide the ability to generate greenhouse gas credits for use in later years, while continuing to improve emissions performance and fuel economy over time.” In addition to the revised emissions timeline, the federal and Ontario governments are investing $2.5 billion over two years to support capital projects by Canadian auto manufacturers.

Reaction to the new policy has been mixed. Climate activists are disappointed to see any retreat from the emissions standards that were in place, since the new rules will undermine the transition to electric cars. Industries hoped the announcement would bring a sense of direction, clarity, and certainty to the future. In any event, Chinese manufacturers are waiting in the wings, as Canada has opened a door for up to 49,000 Chinese EVs to be imported with only a 6.1 percent tariff.

“[T]he decision to pause any increase in the regulation until model year 2030 puts significantly more pressure on the policy’s later years and could undermine success down the road,” Clean Energy Canada said in a statement. “The unexpected delay will impact the potential benefits of stronger EV uptake, including thousands in fuel cost savings for households and up to $21 billion in charging industry investments. At the same time, Canadian communities will face the increased health costs and impacts from worse air quality.”

Pembina Institute , a British Columbia based clean energy advocacy group, took issue with the new policy, claiming it will make it virtually impossible for Canada to achieve its EV goals. “Earlier this year, the federal government promised stronger vehicle pollution standards starting in 2027, but they are now delaying that to 2029. This makes its goal of 75 per cent EVs by 2035 next to impossible, delaying progress toward giving Canadians more affordable vehicle choices.”

title: New Bentley Supersports Convertible Will Carry On A Silly Yet Awesome Legacy
raw_summary: I think that one of the coolest cars of the 2000s is the first-generation Bentley Continental Supersports. The British automaker took its big GT coupe and made it as rowdy as possible, packing in some surprising lightweighting measures and incredible Piëch-era engineering changes. There was an Supersports version of the second-generation Continental as well, and both models were offered in convertible guise, a silly and incongruous but fully awesome proposition. Bentley removed the rear seats for the Supersports coupes, but the convertibles kept in the small back seat — especially fun on the first-gen car, which was available with the carbon-fiber bucket seats from the Bugatti Veyron up front. Going for the convertible lessened the Supersports' weight savings (and was a bit less sporty in general due to the nature of droptops), and it took a certain kind of buyer to find it appealing.

There was an Supersports version of the second-generation Continental as well, and both models were offered in convertible guise, a silly and incongruous but fully awesome proposition.

Bentley removed the rear seats for the Supersports coupes, but the convertibles kept in the small back seat — especially fun on the first-gen car, which was available with the carbon-fiber bucket seats from the Bugatti Veyron up front. Going for the convertible lessened the Supersports' weight savings (and was a bit less sporty in general due to the nature of droptops), and it took a certain kind of buyer to find it appealing.

Now we know Bentley will be continuing on this ridiculous and amazing tradition with the new Supersports , and it'll be the wildest one yet. The fourth-generation Supersports coupe is Bentley's lightest car in 85 years and the first rear-wheel-drive Conti since the '90s, and by far its sportiest offering ever. If you want a big luxurious convertible that's also dynamically inclined and exciting to drive, the new Bentley Supersports convertible will be your only real option.

There's not really a lot to say here. It looks like a convertible version of the Supersports. It's got the same wild carbon-fiber bodykit and prominent rear spoiler, which actually have aerodynamic and performance benefits. We can see the quad exhaust tips that will make a great noise, and a boring Y-spoke wheel design. Sadly the new Supersports doesn't have Bugatti seats, but its carbon-backed front seats are quite nice, and present on this prototype; though the area is all covered up, there's definitely a pair of back seats there, too.

The Supersports coupe is more than 300 pounds lighter than the old V8-powered Continental GT and around 1,100 pounds lighter than a current plug-in-hybrid Conti GT , and those figures will probably hold pretty close for the convertible. That means the droptop Supersports should come in around 4,700 pounds, or about 1,400 pounds heavier than the Porsche 911 GT3 S/C , the kinda-closest equivalent to it. Bentley is only making 500 of the Supersports coupe and they all sold out within a couple months of the car being shown, so I bet the convertible will match that number.

In the 1990s, the vast majority of Plymouth's lineup consisted of badge-engineered versions of various Japanese cars or leftover Dodge products, and it was still only able to muster up about half of Dodge's sales. At the very end, the retro-modern-styled Prowler was the brand's only true Plymouth-designed model.

When it was finally put on the chopping block in 1999, Plymouth was simply not a part of Chrysler's future plans. Done and dusted. But nobody really cares that Plymouth went out at a low point — it's not like we judge Michael Jordan's career based on his final seasons with the Washington Wizards, right? Right.

Plymouth, despite its quiet and underwhelming demise, was a pillar of the American auto industry and delivered some of the most timeless Mopars of the 20th century, some of which you may be interested in for yourself. If that's the case (or if you're simply curious about values), we've conjured up a mix of desirable and important Plymouths, each with an up-to-date estimated value from Hagerty for you to compare against your bank account... and your better judgment.

In contrast to the bleak 1990s version of Plymouth, mid-1950s Plymouth was convincingly in the fight for industry-leading sales figures. It was one of the top three brands in the U.S. by sales in the early part of this decade, but its hold was slipping, and the Plymouth Fury nameplate was one small part of the plan to get this train back on track. The Fury first arrived in 1956 as the high-performance trim of Plymouth's full-size Belvedere. For three model years, the Fury name continued as a mere option (these "sub-series" Belvedere Fury models are actually quite rare), but in 1959, the Fury was spun off as a standalone model.

But now, the Fury itself needed a high-performance trim; hence, the Sport Fury. It only came in two-door configurations, with a hardtop and a slightly more expensive convertible option for those in sunny climates. And because it was the king-of-the-hill version of the Fury, the Sport Fury ditched the typical 230-horsepower two-barrel-carbureted 318 V8 and opted for the four-barrel, 260-horsepower version of the 318 V8 as the standard engine option. There was even an optional 361-cubic-inch "Golden Commando" V8, which boosted the Sport Fury's output to 305 horsepower.

Aside from the motors, the 1959 Sport Fury was a slick piece of machinery at the time, featuring an air-powered leveling system for the rear suspension, swiveling seats (safety first, of course), and an automatically dimming rear-view mirror, among others. In 1959, a Sport Fury cost just under $3,000 (around $30,000 in today's money). Coincidentally, for a good-condition Sport Fury equipped with its standard 318 V8, the estimated value today comes out to around $30,000.

The Plymouth GTX, also known as " the gentleman's muscle car ," appeared right in the midst of the whirlwind of Mopar muscle competition in the mid-to-late 1960s. There was the Satellite, Barracuda, Charger, and eventually the Road Runner, Duster, and Challenger, all vying for the hearts and wallets of those partial to a bit of straight-line speed. And because this came before the Road Runner, the GTX was Plymouth's first real attempt at making a hot Belvedere-based muscle car.

But the GTX isn't just special because it was one of Plymouth's very first attempts at a high-performance automobile. Rather, it's because the GTX never settled for dipping a mere toe into the horsepower wars — it dove straight in. Like LeBron James going directly from high school to the NBA, the GTX's standard engine was the 375-horsepower "Super Commando" 440-cubic-inch V8. Additionally, the only optional engine aside from the standard 440 was the venerable 426 Hemi — quite a brochure, no?

article_paragraphs: Even though Subaru is a Japanese company, many models are built in the United States

Subaru is one of Japan's automotive juggernauts. Established in 1953, it revealed its first model, the 1500, the following year and launched the mass-market 360 in 1958. The company is as Japanese as origami and cherry blossoms, but that doesn't mean it only builds cars in Japan. In fact, Subaru also manufactures vehicles right here in the United States.

Car companies often build vehicles in several countries. For example, Toyota has factories in Japan, Thailand, India, the U.S., Canada, Mexico, France, Poland, and Brazil, among others. Subaru's reach doesn't extend as far, as it builds cars only in its home country and the U.S.

Subaru arrived in the U.S. in 1968, and the popularity of its models surged in the 1970s. As sales rose, Subaru realized it'd be wise to start building cars locally and opened the Subaru of Indiana Automotive (SIA) plant in 1989. More than six million cars have been built at this site, and if you drive a Subaru in the U.S., there's a good chance it was built locally.

The largest model Subaru builds in the U.S. is the Ascent. The three-row SUV comes in seven- and eight-seat configurations and is built exclusively at the Lafayette plant. Subaru launched the Ascent as a successor to the Tribeca in 2018, and while it's now almost a decade old , it still remains surprisingly popular. In fact, sales through the first nine months of this year were up 3.9% from 2025, with 32,556 sold.

Subaru's Indiana plant also produces the Crosstrek . This has long been one of the company's best-selling products in the U.S. and is now in its third generation. From January to September this year, Subaru sold 142,725 units, making it the brand's second best-selling model behind the Forester.

Speaking of the Forester, it is also made in the U.S. Production of the new hybrid Forester kicked off at the Indiana plant in February, while the gas-powered model has been built locally for the past year. Subaru hasn't historically built the Forester in the U.S., as all previous generations were made in Japan. Subaru only recently started local production of it to fill the void left behind by the Outback, which had been built in the U.S. but has now shifted back to Japan. Subaru also built the Legacy in the U.S., but local production ended last September.

raw_title: Who's At Fault When Software Glitches Cause A Car Accident?
title: Who's At Fault When Software Glitches Cause A Car Accident?
raw_summary: We're increasingly living in an era when flawed code is causing cars to break. That's according to an analysis by the group Recall Masters ' May, 2026 report. Last year the National Highway Transportation Association (NHTSA) issued a stunning 8 million recalls involving faulty electronics. Many were related to buggy back-up cameras, misfiring driver assistance systems and blipping instrument clusters. We don't know exactly how many fewer bricked cars this would amount to if it weren't for Ford's many recalls delaying dealer fixes, but that's a different headache. Actually, maybe it's related. Because if any not-yet-repaired software-blipping car harmed the driver, passenger, a pedestrian or anyone else outside the vehicle, we wanted to know who'd be responsible. Is it the driver? What about the shop that made the last software patch? And, naturally, how about the car's manufacturer?
summary: We're increasingly living in an era when flawed code is causing cars to break. That's according to an analysis by the group Recall Masters ' May, 2026 report. Last year the National Highway Transportation Association (NHTSA) issued a stunning 8 million recalls involving faulty electronics.
article_paragraphs: We're increasingly living in an era when flawed code is causing cars to break. That's according to an analysis by the group Recall Masters ' May, 2026 report. Last year the National Highway Transportation Association (NHTSA) issued a stunning 8 million recalls involving faulty electronics. Many were related to buggy back-up cameras, misfiring driver assistance systems and blipping instrument clusters. We don't know exactly how many fewer bricked cars this would amount to if it weren't for Ford's many recalls delaying dealer fixes, but that's a different headache.

Actually, maybe it's related. Because if any not-yet-repaired software-blipping car harmed the driver, passenger, a pedestrian or anyone else outside the vehicle, we wanted to know who'd be responsible. Is it the driver? What about the shop that made the last software patch? And, naturally, how about the car's manufacturer?

Since we're not lawyers, and are explicitly not issuing legal advice with this column, we instead asked Charles Gilman, founding attorney of the practice, Gilman of Gilman & Bedigian, LLC , with offices in Maryland, Pennsylvania and Texas. His firm has a focus on medical malpractice, but also intellectual property and automotive claims. His first answer will annoy you — but don't worry, because we didn't let him off that easily.

"This is going to depend on the glitch," he said when asked who would be at fault, "what caused the glitch, and several other factors. For example, if it's a brand new car... the issue may be a software defect, which will point to the manufacturer for liability. If it was a faulty repair or incomplete update, failure to update a known defect of the software liability will rest with the dealership or repair shop that could have [or] should have fixed it."

One question we have has to do with recalls and the responsibility of the car's driver when a recall is issued. Pity the poor Ford owner here, but not solely them. Last year Carfax said there were 54.6 million vehicles with unrepaired recalls nationwide, and this past spring they made that number a bit starker, noting that one in five vehicles on American roads has an unfixed recall. FYI, here's how you can check if your car is subject to a recall .

Now, let's say you never click on that link. Let's say you moved and never got that recall in the mail. Or, for instance, you bought a used car and don't service it at the dealer. Maybe you even do a bunch of repairs yourself, so unlike a decent independent mechanic, you're not actively searching for recalls that they would see when they rotate your tires. Really, should it be on you, the car's owner, to know if your car was designed properly? And what about the upsides and downsides of over-the-air updates ? Should you be on the hook for knowing if your slick ride is even getting those, which, theoretically, should mean fewer software glitches?

Gliman says the manufacturer probably still has more liability than you do when it comes to recalls. Put simply, just issuing a recall wouldn't by default protect the carmaker from liability in the event of an accident. "Recall notices will not necessarily release the manufacturer from claims," he says. "They may have to issue orders to stop using the vehicle depending on the defect."

Gilman can't see a scenario where a car buyer would be held at fault for purchasing the wrong car, such as one with open recalls or stop-drive orders from the manufacturer. "It would be the seller of the vehicle that should know and has the best ability to know that the vehicle should not have been sold," Gillman explains. "If the vehicle has known defects, the manufacturer and the dealership are in the best position to prevent the sale of the vehicle, so the liability should rest with them."

He reasoned that the $4,500 he spent on the car would quickly be made up by his daily local trips. He was offloading his low-mileage used AWD Dodge Charger. Rising operating costs for the Dodge, including insurance rates, oil changes, and tires (on top of mounting Stellantis maintenance bills), plus the extra set of winter tires and L2 wall charger that came with the Nissan meant the car would pay for itself in short order. This friend is a dyed-in-the-wool car nut. He has a collection of hot rods and a self-built shop space with several times more square footage than my home. When I need help tuning a carburetor or fabricating fender flares, he's the guy I call. The fact that he's been converted to the merits of electric vehicles in these trying times is, anecdotally at least, indicative of changing trends in the car market. This friend is no luddite, but he's not the sort to adopt the latest technology without good reason.

title: Hey! Pay Attention! Drivers Find Multitasking Tough When Using Touchscreens, Says Study

According to a recent University of Washington study, trying to keep your car on the road while also tapping on a digital display leads to greater lane drift among 16 experienced drivers tested on a simulator. article_paragraphs: Here's a shocker: Tapping a touchscreen while driving makes you lousy at both tasks. According to a recent University of Washington study, trying to keep your car on the road while also tapping on a digital display leads to greater lane drift among 16 experienced drivers tested on a simulator. In fact, the study found that weaving like a drunk driver — or one with a hangover, which apparently is also dangerous — increased by a pretty substantial 41.9% on average. The tested drivers also got 58% worse at finding the input they were hunting for on the touchscreen.

You are probably already aware that distracted driving is dangerous — very dangerous. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), it led to 3,208 deaths in 2024. And according to the agency's tracking, in that year alone, distracted driving contributed to another 315,167 injuries on the road. And, unfortunately, some automakers like BMW claim to be responding to younger buyer demands by ditching physical buttons and pesky knobs. Meanwhile, NHTSA data shows that drivers between the ages of 25 and 34 comprised the most dangerous people on the road — they make up 22% of distracted drivers and 27% of drivers distracted by cellphones during fatal crashes.

A separate Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) study out in August shows that police drastically undercount the involvement of cell phone distraction when they file accident reports. The IIHS says that number may be higher by a factor of seven after the non-profit instead used vehicle telematics to re-survey 17,000 crashes between 2021 and 2024. Distraction by IIHS's measure includes both passive and active use, such as interaction with navigation apps, though IIHS notes that a quarter of participants in a separate study admitted to watching a video on their phones while driving within the past 30 days.

You know how automakers think, right? They'll just make the on-screen buttons bigger so they're easier to tap. Sadly, the University of Washington researchers found that doesn't help. According to the researchers, we aren't equipped to adequately handle the complex task of driving and then glancing away from the road and onto a screen to find the widget, button, or volume knob while, say, tracing the curvature of the road or the brake lights ahead. The researchers instead suggest that screens need to be designed to anticipate what users are looking for, or in their language, to enhance visual saliency, such as by using ambient lighting adjustments or "subtle animations to draw attention to actionable elements." Another aspect of the study was to look at multi-step tasks.

The more we have to pay attention to a primary cognitive task, the less able we are to also drill deeply through nested menu structures, and the more time this consumes. The University of Washington researchers suggest a remedy for this by "flattening" the number of steps to complete an action, and suggest that "frequently used functions should be surfaced as one-tap actions when high cognitive load is detected." While there are efforts to reduce distracting elements in vehicles, automakers tend to default to warning drivers that they're distracted, such as by using eye- and head-tracking. But that doesn't fix the underlying issue of what's causing the distraction in the first place — the difficulty of using a touchscreen during driving.

To make interfaces safer, the authors of the University of Washington study suggest it would be better to monitor what's happening to the driver and then adapt the in-car tech in response to the distraction. They'd do this by using more in-depth measurements than just tracking our head or eye movements. In their study, they measured eye-tracking, skin temperature, and pupil dilation as well as eye movement and live task performance. In theory, then, menus might get simpler when we're stressed by the act of driving.

Not to belittle the University of Washington findings, but they're not exactly groundbreaking. For example, a 2018 AAA and University of Utah study found that both Apple CarPlay and Android Auto were less stressful for drivers inputting touchscreen tasks like sending a text than five automakers' native systems, but still cognitively demanding. However, another 2020 study by the U.K.'s Transport Research Laboratory found that both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay cause significant distraction, with participants struggling to drive a simulator while using them. For instance, drivers using Android Auto spent as much as 20 seconds in total with their eyes off the road while trying to tune to a specific Spotify playlist. And their reaction times slowed by as much as 53%.

Many drivers still have a preference for physical buttons, and perhaps that's the solution. And in Europe, the New Car Assessment Program (NCAP) now mandates that some functions be "operated by a direct physical input rather than a touchscreen," and it seems touchscreen-only interfaces are too distracting to receive five-star safety ratings there . In fact, NCAP calls touchscreens "needlessly fiddly," and says research has shown a "higher distraction potential for a driver compared to physical buttons."

title: How Long Should You Let Your Car Idle After A Jump Start?
raw_summary: Is it ok to remove the leads right after the car starts or should you wait? A flat battery is downright annoying, seriously stressful, and hard to fix without the right help or equipment. Older, lighter, manual-transmission cars can be bump- or push-started by dropping the clutch to force the engine to spin, once you've built up enough speed with the help of a hill, or a friend to push you along. Reviving a heavier car on flat ground, or an automatic, though, will require jumper cables. But how long should you leave the engine running once you've brought it back from the dead?
summary: Is it ok to remove the leads right after the car starts or should you wait? A flat battery is downright annoying, seriously stressful, and hard to fix without the right help or equipment. Older, lighter, manual-transmission cars can be bump- or push-started by dropping the clutch to force the engine to spin, once you've built up enough speed with the help of a hill, or a friend to push you along.
article_paragraphs: Is it ok to remove the leads right after the car starts or should you wait?

A flat battery is downright annoying, seriously stressful, and hard to fix without the right help or equipment. Older, lighter, manual-transmission cars can be bump- or push-started by dropping the clutch to force the engine to spin, once you've built up enough speed with the help of a hill, or a friend to push you along. Reviving a heavier car on flat ground, or an automatic, though, will require jumper cables. But how long should you leave the engine running once you've brought it back from the dead?

The answer depends on several factors, including the battery size, how flat it was when you jumped it, and how much load you'll put on it in the minutes after restarting. A car's battery is charged by its alternator, a small generator driven by a belt off the engine's crankshaft. But an alternator generates only a small current when the engine is idling, enough to run a car's ignition, fuel injection, dashboard and electric power steering (where fitted), but not enough to meaningfully charge a dead battery.

You can boost the alternator's output by increasing the engine revs a little while still parked up, but your best plan is to get driving once you're sure the engine is running properly. Battery experts generally recommend driving at highway speeds for around 30 minutes while using no electrical accessories, to put enough charge in a battery to ensure it'll start again safely once you've switched it off. But if it's dark and rainy, and you're running the headlights, wipers, AC, and blasting music from your custom 36-speaker, four-amp sound system, you're going to need to put some more miles under your wheels.

Modern cars are much more complicated beasts than their ancestors, and while they can still be jump-started , the method is probably a little different from the one your dad learned years ago. But the starting point is the same. You need a donor "jumper" car that you can park near enough to reach cables between it and the dead car.

The traditional jump method was to connect each end of the red cable to the positive terminal on each car's battery. Then connect the negative cable to the donor car's negative terminal, then snap the jaws from the other end around the dead car's negative terminal. That's bad news for modern vehicles, because a sudden spike in current can fry their engine control unit (ECU) brain.

So the modern advice is to connect the positive cable as before, and one end of the negative lead to the donor car's battery, but to clip the other end to an earth point in the dead car's engine bay. Some cars have dedicated earth points, but if not, you'll usually find some other metal fitting that will work.

With the cables secure, wait a couple of minutes, then start the working car's engine and leave it running for another minute or two. Now try to start the dead car. If it fires, great. If not, wait a few more minutes, then give it another go. Once the car with the flat battery is up and running, the temptation is to whip the leads off right away. But don't. Leave the leads in place for a few minutes with both cars running before taking them off in the reverse order.

raw_title: Energy Transition Plans Keep Freezing Today’s Demand Into Tomorrow
title: Energy Transition Plans Keep Freezing Today’s Demand Into Tomorrow
raw_summary: A lot of energy-transition analysis begins with an assumption that is easy to miss: the size and shape of today’s market are carried into the future. Once that happens, the analytical task becomes finding a low-carbon substitute for everything the incumbent system currently supplies. That approach can make the replacement problem much larger than it needs to be. Industries change as the energy transition proceeds, technologies compete across sector boundaries, demand responds to price, and some of the commodities that dominate today’s energy system shrink for reasons that have little to do with the technology being proposed as their replacement.

Once that happens, the analytical task becomes finding a low-carbon substitute for everything the incumbent system currently supplies. That approach can make the replacement problem much larger than it needs to be.
article_paragraphs: A lot of energy-transition analysis begins with an assumption that is easy to miss: the size and shape of today’s market are carried into the future. Once that happens, the analytical task becomes finding a low-carbon substitute for everything the incumbent system currently supplies.

That approach can make the replacement problem much larger than it needs to be. Industries change as the energy transition proceeds, technologies compete across sector boundaries, demand responds to price, and some of the commodities that dominate today’s energy system shrink for reasons that have little to do with the technology being proposed as their replacement.

I discussed this recently with Amy Rennison at an Earth Set event at Octopus Energy’s London headquarters. The conversation covered shipping, hydrogen, grids, heat pumps, aviation, carbon removal and data centres, with questions from the audience repeatedly pulling us back to the assumptions underneath apparently confident transition forecasts. I expanded the discussion in The Energy Transition Has An Assumptions Problem .

Shipping is a good place to see the problem. Roughly 40% of maritime freight tonnage is coal, oil and gas, with raw iron ore accounting for another 15%. Fossil-fuel demand declines as energy systems electrify, steel production changes, and inland and short-sea routes increasingly become candidates for battery electrification. All of those changes affect the amount of liquid fuel the shipping industry will eventually require.

My projection leaves about 70 million tonnes of annual shipping fuel demand by 2100. Other projections reach several hundred million tonnes. That gap has enormous consequences for investment because it changes how much biomass, synthetic fuel, renewable electricity and supporting infrastructure appear necessary. A fuel pathway that looks impossibly constrained against one demand forecast can look quite different against another.

The same issue appears when biological fuels are discussed across transport sectors. Cars, trucks and trains electrify, much of shorter-distance shipping can electrify, and fossil-fuel freight declines. Aviation remains a stronger claimant on scarce sustainable liquid fuels, which affects what is economically available to shipping. Looking at those markets together changed my own assessment of how much biodiesel and renewable diesel should appear in my maritime pathway.

Hydrogen provides a different example of assumptions shaping investment. The broad hydrogen-economy narrative depended heavily on green hydrogen becoming inexpensive enough to compete in transportation, heating, electricity storage and a wide range of industrial applications. I kept working through production and delivery economics and found a much smaller addressable market when hydrogen remained expensive.

Policies, subsidy programmes, corporate organizations and investment plans had already formed around the larger market expectation. Institutions do not disappear as quickly as the assumptions that created them. Once money, staff and political commitments accumulate around a proposition, changing direction becomes an organizational problem as well as an analytical one.

Once that happens, the analytical task becomes finding a low-carbon substitute for everything the incumbent system currently supplies.
That approach can make the replacement problem much larger than it needs to be.

raw_title: 5 Cool Facts About The Ecto-1 Every Ghostbusters Fan Should Know
title: 5 Cool Facts About The Ecto-1 Every Ghostbusters Fan Should Know
raw_summary: The movie Ghostbusters was a flat-out smash when it debuted in 1984, becoming the highest-grossing comedy at the time — until it was replaced by Home Alone in 1990. No doubt helping matters were all the stars attached to the flick, including Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, Sigourney Weaver, Rick Moranis, Harold Ramis, Ernie Hudson, and, of course, the Ecto-1. That last name refers to the Ghostbusters' original support vehicle — a modified 1959 Cadillac wagon that offered enough room for the team's Proton Packs, Ecto Goggles, P.K.E. Meters, and Ghost Traps. Needless to say, the car cast a huge shadow since the film was first released — as you'd expect from a vehicle that's almost 21 feet long – and it still inspires ghost-battling gearheads around the world today. Even Rivian recently got into the action with an R1S featuring officially licensed movie sounds, games, and a spooky voice assistant , as well as an Ecto-style livery.

article_paragraphs: The movie Ghostbusters was a flat-out smash when it debuted in 1984, becoming the highest-grossing comedy at the time — until it was replaced by Home Alone in 1990. No doubt helping matters were all the stars attached to the flick, including Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, Sigourney Weaver, Rick Moranis, Harold Ramis, Ernie Hudson, and, of course, the Ecto-1.

That last name refers to the Ghostbusters' original support vehicle — a modified 1959 Cadillac wagon that offered enough room for the team's Proton Packs, Ecto Goggles, P.K.E. Meters, and Ghost Traps. Needless to say, the car cast a huge shadow since the film was first released — as you'd expect from a vehicle that's almost 21 feet long – and it still inspires ghost-battling gearheads around the world today. Even Rivian recently got into the action with an R1S featuring officially licensed movie sounds, games, and a spooky voice assistant , as well as an Ecto-style livery.

Speaking of which, did you know the original plans for the car would have given it a far different look? Aykroyd, who had worked on early drafts of the script with Ramis, had wanted to use a black car lit up by purple and white strobe lights. But because so much shooting was to be done in the dark of night, when a black vehicle would be tough to film, white was chosen instead. Nor is that the only little-known factoid about the legendary Ecto-1. In fact, we've got five more for you right here.

It's not uncommon for filmmakers to use multiple vehicles behind the scenes to play a single car on-screen. For example, for the classic gearhead flick "Gone in 60 Seconds," it turns out that 11 different cars were used to play Eleanor in the film — don't worry, though, as no actual Shelby GT500s were harmed during shooting .

Now, two different Cadillac-based Miller-Meteor vehicles did appear in the original "Ghostbusters." But the first, a rental wearing a coat of black primer, basically played the donor car for what would become the Ecto-1. In the movie, the black car is upgraded into proper ghost-busting condition to become the Ecto-1. In the real world, however, it went back to the rental agency, and the second car took on the role. That said, after the initial Ecto-1 broke down during filming of "Ghostbusters II," earning the production crew a fine, the crew brought in a third car and modified it to fill in for the rest of the movie. As for the Ecto-1, it was reportedly ignominiously dumped on a studio lot, where it languished, exposed to the elements for almost 18 years. It was eventually restored by Cinema Vehicles and used to promote its 2009 Ghostbusters video game.

It was actually both! While the media often describes the car underpinning the Ecto-1 as a Cadillac ambulance, that's not the whole story. The car is a Cadillac Miller-Meteor Futura Duplex, one of an estimated 400 built for 1959, and the Duplex name refers to its two potential functions — the same car can fairly quickly switch from ambulance to hearse or vice versa. Its secret seems to have been a rear compartment with ambulance-attendant seats that could fold into the floor, which in turn can be flipped over to hide or expose casket rollers as needed.

The Miller-Meteor part of the equation is explained by the company behind the conversion. The coachbuilder was formed when a bus company called the Wayne Works (later Wayne Corporation) purchased Miller and then, separately Meteor — two rivals in the livery car market. Merging the two helped create what was, for a time, the world's largest manufacturer of hearses and ambulances.

To be clear, though, while Miller-Meteor handled much of the bodywork, its foundation was a heavy-duty commercial chassis from Cadillac that was in production from 1931 to 1979. This was part of Cadillac's long history of building funeral cars , and it meant that only the front bodywork was from the factory — well, that and its rear tailfins. They were borrowed from the 1959 Cadillac Eldorado and are still the biggest ones to ever appear on a production vehicle.

title: Wide Vs Narrow Tires: Is One Better For Off-Road Performance?
raw_summary: If you're looking to maximize the off-road performance of your rock-crawler for capability as well as Instagram likes, you might head straight for the tallest, fattest tire you can stuff under your rig. Now some of you may be having flashbacks to previous botched, over the top "upgrades," and asking: "in the name of off-road performance, how big is too big?" The spectrum of an off-roader's tire diameter choice may range from "manufacturer's recommendation" to " what will physically fit and not break anything in its current setup?" Sure, a larger diameter or taller tire will offer increased ground clearance, approach, departure, breakover angles, better tire attack angles (ease at rolling over obstacles), and make the vehicle look less like it's en pointe. When choosing a tire width, bigger is better too, right? Well, not exactly.
summary: If you're looking to maximize the off-road performance of your rock-crawler for capability as well as Instagram likes, you might head straight for the tallest, fattest tire you can stuff under your rig.
article_paragraphs: If you're looking to maximize the off-road performance of your rock-crawler for capability as well as Instagram likes, you might head straight for the tallest, fattest tire you can stuff under your rig. Now some of you may be having flashbacks to previous botched, over the top "upgrades," and asking: "in the name of off-road performance, how big is too big?"

The spectrum of an off-roader's tire diameter choice may range from "manufacturer's recommendation" to " what will physically fit and not break anything in its current setup?" Sure, a larger diameter or taller tire will offer increased ground clearance, approach, departure, breakover angles, better tire attack angles (ease at rolling over obstacles), and make the vehicle look less like it's en pointe. When choosing a tire width, bigger is better too, right? Well, not exactly.

Against common perception, increasing tire width does not always increase grip off road. The contact patch (area of tire physically on the ground) does not change when increasing width, only the shape. Short and wide (hamburger-shaped) for a wide tire vs long & thin (hotdog-shaped) for a narrower tire. The contact patch shape from a wide vs narrow tire is a product of tire width yields better performance in specific conditions. Choosing the best performing tire width will depend on your use case.

Wider tires aren't just for doing an impression of your favorite predator themed off-roader. Wide tires perform well on terrain you'd want to "float" on: loose surfaces with no hard-packed terrain below such as loose sand and deep, deep mud. Running a wider tire can also offer protection for your precious rims by protruding from the rim and keeping rocks a little farther from the wheels. Remember that "hamburger" contact patch? That wider contact patch provides increased lateral grip for higher horsepower vehicles, maintaining stability during heavy acceleration both on and off-road. Ultimately, in a lot of cases, wider tires are chosen for their beefier looks and improved aesthetics.

On the other hand, narrow tires outperform wide tires in shallow, loose, wet surfaces with hard terrain underneath. Think snow, shallow mud, and rain. The "hotdog" narrow and long contact patch's leading edge (the first part of the contact patch that hits the road as the tire spins) acts like a knife cutting through loose surfaces so the rest of the contact patch can grip to the solid terrain below. The longer contact patch also can act like a caterpillar or tank track over uneven terrain when aired down.

Narrower tires also offer several quality of life improvements for both on and off the trail. When compared to the equivalent wider tire, the narrower tire will be lighter. Lighter is good! With less rotational inertia, less engine power is required to get them rolling and less brakes are required to get them stopping. This equates to better mpg and more range for your excursions. Less unsprung weight will allow the suspension to do its job easier giving you a smoother, potentially quieter ride. Less physical tire size is easier to install and less likely to hit body or suspension components without adding a lift or other modifications. The cherry on top of choosing a slimmer tire: less money ! The lighter tires put less wear and tear on your vehicle and are generally cheaper to purchase.

Tire size will, in part, dictate your rig's ability to get through your chosen trail, but tread and sidewall design are equally important. A tire with a more flexible composition or ability to conform around objects allows the tire to mold around terrain. This effectively increases the contact patch around objects instead of just on top of them like on flat pavement. Specialized, softer tires with increased capabilities come at the cost of on road stability, quietness, & tread life as compared to a more rigid on-road or all-terrain tire.

Two free tricks that can be used on your current set of tires are airing down and adding load. Airing down is when a driver purposely lets out 10-15 psi from their tires to deflate and soften the tires. Without getting into the math, a lower tire pressure inversely increases the contact patch of the tire. This means more tire on the ground, and more grip over that obstacle. Pair this with a softer, more flexible tire design for maximum off-road performance. Added bonuses from the lower tire pressure: smoother ride quality over the rough stuff and you're less likely to get a flat as the tire can conform better to rocks.

raw_summary: Ferrari has arrived in Austin with what should be its last Formula 1 car update of 2026. From what we can see, it’s not a massive change - just small changes to the details in various areas, but as I often say, they all add up.

From what we can see, it’s not a massive change - just small changes to the details in various areas, but as I often say, they all add up.

To be honest, Ferrari has not been that far behind as far as performance is concerned. It's been points lost through execution and decision-making. I know that Lewis Hamilton put his hand up as to not pitting under the VSC in Singapore, for instance, but that’s just one example of Ferrari's indecisions costing it.

Without doubt, Hamilton has lots of experience when it comes to making pit calls - some good, some bad - but my concern with the driver overruling the team is that for any driver, they only have their own information, and at most that of the cars in front and behind them, as to what the tyre situation is. The team has - or at least should have - the information from all of the cars still running, so a much broader picture of what is happening, so it should be able to make a better decision.

I say 'should' here because I have no idea if Ferrari looks any further than its own cars and also there seems to be a bit of a reluctance for anyone to put their heads above the parapet. If you don’t make decisions, you can never be held responsible for making the wrong decision.
Ferrari has also thrown away quite a few points by not allowing whatever driver is fastest to just press on - again, that falls into the reactiveness of decision making.
Anyway, that’s my moan for today - onto the developments. As I said, from what I can see, it is small detail changes.

The purple fin separating the radiator intake from the coke bottle undercut seems to have increased in size slightly. As the car speed increases, the radiator will not be able to flow the volume of air that is presented to it - when this happens, the inlet duct will start to spill around the outer body surface. This fin will reduce the adverse effect this spillage would have on the undercut sidepod.
